fundamental.thesis: Titan is India's largest organised jewellery retailer (Tanishq, CaratLane, Mia; about 8.5% share of organised retail) and also leads in watches (27% analog share) and is the number two organised eyewear chain, with 3,758 stores. Q2FY27 revenue was ₹20,533 cr, up 25.1% YoY, which is faster than the first half overall (H1 ₹41,970 cr, +19.1%, so Q1 was about +13-14%), helped by studded jewellery growing 32%, jewellery same-store growth of 15%, and margin gains in watches (+27% revenue) and eyecare (+28%). However, the H1 PAT of ₹4,170 cr (+88.6%, 9.9% margin) is boosted by one-offs: ₹536 cr of customs duty benefits and a ₹671 cr reduction in the Damas option liability. H1 operating cash flow was negative at -2.68x PAT (FCF -₹11,585 cr), almost certainly from building up gold inventory. Q2 PAT was not extracted, so the latest-quarter margin cannot be confirmed. On valuation, trailing P/E is 74.3x and forward P/E is 49.4x, which sits inside the 60-100x premium band the sector card sets for top consumer franchises, so I grade it fair. The peer screen does show it as expensive (EV/EBITDA 48x vs a 21.9x median, P94), but that peer set is mostly autos and is not a like-for-like comparison. The biggest risks are that jewellery buyer count was flat YoY, so growth depends on bigger ticket sizes and gold prices, and that the earnings are both inflated by one-offs and not yet turning into cash.

fundamental.thesis: Kotak Mahindra Bank is one of India's largest private-sector banks, with a strong capital base (CET1 22.1%) and growing wealth and asset-management arms (customer AUM ₹8.14L cr, +8% YoY). Profit growth has picked up sharply: consolidated PAT rose 26.3% YoY to ₹5,645 cr in Q2FY27, up from +23.0% in Q1FY27 and +5.0% in Q3FY26, and standalone NII rose 16% to ₹8,459 cr. Asset quality has improved steadily, with GNPA falling from 1.39% to 1.04% over five periods and slippages down 24%, but this quarter's growth comes partly off a weak base (Q2FY26 PAT was -2.7%), and NIM fell 23bps YoY to 4.31% as costlier FCNR(B) deposits came in. On the bank yardstick (P/B plus ROE, not P/E), a P/B of 2.08x against an ROE of only 11.4-11.7% is fair, not cheap; it sits at the 86th percentile among bank peers on both P/B and forward P/E (13.6x), so it already carries a premium that its current ROE does not clearly earn. The biggest risk is margin squeeze: falling NIM, CASA slipping from 42.3% to 41.8%, a 4.52% cost of funds and an 8.1% cut to next-FY EPS estimates while 32 of 37 analysts still rate it a buy, a pattern that often comes before a re-rating lower.

fundamental.thesis: TCS is India's largest IT services company (₹8L cr market cap, near-debt-free with filing-reported D/E 0.099 and ROE 51%), serving global clients across BFSI (39.1% of revenue), Manufacturing, and Consumer verticals with dominant scale and 12-year consecutive top-ranked customer satisfaction. Revenue re-accelerated sharply in H1 FY27 to ₹1,45,463 cr (+12.6% YoY, with Q1FY27 at +13.9%), up from a sluggish +4.6% in FY26, and PAT margins expanded from 15.9% in Q3FY26 to 18.8% in H1 FY27 — but the critical flag is that FY26 constant-currency growth was -2.4%, meaning the INR headline re-acceleration is substantially FX-tailwind-driven (INR/USD ~94.96 vs ~84 in FY26) rather than evidence of genuine organic demand recovery; EBITDA margins have also contracted from 28.7% to 27.2%, and deferred revenue declined ₹1,092 cr QoQ, both pointing to margin and pipeline softening beneath the headline beat. At 16.3× trailing P/E — a 33.7% discount to the IT sector peer median of 24.7× and cheapest in sector on forward P/E at 13.4× — TCS screens unambiguously cheap versus both sector peers and the benchmark range of 22–30×, with a pristine balance sheet (CFO/PAT 0.94×, FCF ₹23,768 cr in H1) providing a durable floor; the P/E yardstick is used here as primary per the asset-light IT services model, and EV/EBITDA at 11.1× (P17 in sector vs median 14.7×) corroborates the cheap read. The central risk is AI-led productivity deflation continuing to compress legacy T&M revenues in constant-currency terms: if INR stabilises from current weakness, CC growth likely reverts to near-zero or negative, the INR acceleration collapses, and the re-rating catalyst disappears, leaving TCS cheap but with no near-term earnings growth to close the discount.

fundamental.thesis: Hindalco is a global aluminium and copper producer: it makes primary aluminium in India, owns Novelis (the world's largest maker of rolled aluminium products) and runs a large copper business, so its earnings swing with LME metal prices. Q2FY27 revenue hit a record ₹91,708 cr, up 38.8% YoY, faster than Q1's +32.0%. PAT reached a record ₹7,533 cr, up 58.9%, but PAT growth slowed from +75.2% in Q1, and EBITDA margin fell from 17.7% to 15.0% quarter on quarter as the Novelis Oswego fire costs hit. The PAT jump was also helped by about 150 bps from a lower tax rate. For a cyclical, the right yardstick is EV/EBITDA. At 9.3x, Hindalco is cheap against its broad Materials peers (P7, median 17.9x), but that median is pushed up by paint makers. Against the 5–8x mid-cycle range for metal producers, it is somewhat rich for a business near peak LME prices. Trailing P/E of 18.2x sits inside the 12–22x band, forward P/E is 10.3x, and the stock is at 85% of its 52-week range, so overall valuation is fair, not cheap. The main worry is that strong profits are not yet turning into cash: H1 operating cash flow was only 0.19x PAT, free cash flow was -₹16,519 cr, and net debt/EBITDA rose to 1.80x from 1.23x a year ago, with capex set to rise further in FY28.

fundamental.thesis: Dr Reddy's is a large Indian generics maker with heavy US exposure, plus a fast-growing India branded business and emerging-market and biosimilar franchises. The latest quarter extracted from filings is Q1 FY27; Q2 FY27 results were filed on 23 Oct but not yet extracted, and the yfinance Q2 revenue of 4,150 cr is about half the normal run-rate, so it is treated as suspect. In Q1 FY27 revenue fell 5.6% YoY to 8,070 cr, down from +3.0% in FY26, and PAT fell 69% to 435 cr (5.4% margin, down from 12.8%), partly because of a 223 cr semaglutide inventory provision. Even after stripping that one-off, US revenue fell 35% while India formulations grew a healthy 17%, and cash conversion was very weak (CFO/PAT 0.23x, FCF of -22 cr). On valuation I used P/E and EV/EBITDA against peers: trailing P/E of 24.8x sits below the 28-40x sector band and at P23 among peers, with forward P/E (19.8x) and P/B (2.8x) both at P8, so the grade is cheap. HAL is India's main state-owned maker of military aircraft and helicopters, with a near-monopoly on domestic defence aviation and an order book of about ₹2,54,538 cr, roughly 7.7 times annual revenue (Q4FY26). For a capital-intensive order-book business I graded valuation mainly on EV/EBITDA: 29.0x against a peer median of 34.0x (P35) is fair. Trailing P/E of 31.1x is near the bottom of its peer group (P6, 42% below median), though still inside the 28–45x sector range, and forward P/E of 25.4x prices in further earnings growth. The main risk is turning the large order book into revenue on time: slow execution or delivery slippage would hold back growth even as orders pile up. fundamental.thesis: Indian Bank is a mid-sized public-sector bank with a ₹8.74L cr deposit base and ₹7.11L cr of advances, and about two-thirds of its loans go to retail, agriculture and MSME borrowers (RAM 65%). In H1FY27 total income grew 16.1% YoY to ₹44,333 cr and PAT grew 28.1% to ₹6,897 cr, but Q2 includes a one-off NSE listing gain of ₹1,387 cr. Stripping it out, underlying PAT growth looks closer to high single digits, and the core trend is mixed. Gross NPA improved from 2.23% to 1.86% to 1.61% with PCR at 98%. Against that, NIM slipped from 3.37% to 3.24%, credit cost rose from 0.21% to 0.47% to 0.71% over three quarters, and deposits are growing slower than loans (12.5% vs 17.5% YoY). Using P/B against ROE (the lender yardstick), 1.44x book for a 15.4% ROE is cheap in absolute terms, but peers are similar: P/B is only at P43 and P/E (9.9x) at P29 among regional banks, so the grade is fair. Analysts raised FY EPS estimates by about 5% over 90 days, which supports the case. The main risk is that loans keep growing faster than deposits, pushing up funding costs and squeezing NIMs further just as credit costs rise.

fundamental.thesis: Coforge is a fast-growing mid-tier Indian IT services firm focused on banking, insurance and travel clients, and it continues to out-grow tier-1 peers. Q2 FY27 revenue was ₹6,171 cr (+53.6% YoY) with PAT of ₹588 cr (+56.5% YoY), quickening from +49.2% revenue growth in Q1 FY27; PAT margin held steady at about 9.5% and EBITDA margin rose slightly to 20.6%. The forward indicators also look strong: the 12-month executable order book is $2.38bn (+45% YoY), Q2 order intake was $1,040mn with 8 large deals signed, and guidance was raised. However, organic constant-currency growth was a much lower 5.2% QoQ in Q1, and the large AI-engineering and data service lines grew only +1.4% and -6.1% YoY, which suggests much of the headline growth is acquisition-led. On valuation, using P/E backed by EV/EBITDA and peer rank as the IT yardstick, trailing P/E of 32.95× is above the 22–30× sector range and at P88 vs peers. Forward P/E of 21.0× and EV/EBITDA of 15.8× (+7.6% vs the peer median, P67) are close to the peer median given roughly 50% growth, so the overall grade is fair rather than cheap. The biggest risk is that growth is mostly acquired rather than organic, with AI-driven deflation of legacy services underneath; a clear slowdown once the acquisition laps would hit the multiple.

fundamental.thesis: Ajanta Pharma is a branded-generics maker focused on chronic therapies: about 66% of revenue comes from branded generics across India (30%), Asia (18%) and Africa (18%), and US generics add 29%. In India it ranks #1 in ophthalmology and is the 4th fastest-growing of the top 25 companies, growing about 1.27x the Indian pharma market (16.7% vs 13.2%). Growth is speeding up. Revenue growth rose from +14% (Q2FY26) to +20% (Q3FY26) and +25% (Q1FY27), and reached about +32.5% in Q2FY27 (₹1,794 cr, implied from H1 ₹3,420 cr less Q1 ₹1,626 cr). Implied Q2 PAT of ₹388 cr is up about 49%, and PAT margin widened to about 21.6% from 19%, though cash conversion is only moderate (CFO/PAT 0.86x in H1). On the healthcare yardstick of trailing P/E plus peer rank, valuation is fair. Trailing P/E of 35.4x sits inside the 28-40x sector band and at P46 vs peers, and forward P/E of 26.3x signals expected earnings growth. EV/EBITDA of 24.3x (P69) and P/B of 8.3x (P77) carry a premium that a 25% ROE broadly justifies. The biggest risk is the 29% US generics exposure: generics are tariff-exempt for now, but the pending US Commerce review of generics plus forex losses already hitting reported profit could stall the margin gains, and management has given no forward guidance.

Aadhar Housing Finance is a mid-sized affordable-housing lender with an AUM of ₹32,643 cr, 632+ branches across 23 states and an average loan size of about ₹11 lakh, so it serves lower-income home buyers. In Q2 FY27, revenue grew 16.8% YoY to ₹1,048 cr and PAT grew 15.7% to ₹308 cr. PAT growth has slowed from +19.0% in Q1 to +15.7%, and AUM growth has eased from 20% in FY26 to 18% (20% on the company's adjusted basis), even though the PAT margin rose to 29.4% and management maintained its 20% AUM and PAT growth guidance. For a lender we value on P/B against ROE rather than P/E: 2.8x book for a 15.0–15.8% ROE (with ROA above 4%) is fair, not a bargain, for affordable-housing finance. The 19.6x trailing P/E only looks cheap against the broad market because no close housing-finance peers are in the universe. The main risk is asset quality: gross NPA rose from 1.08% at FY26 to 1.35% while provision coverage is only about 34.5%, so any further rise in bad loans would hit earnings quickly.

Q2 FY27 PAT rose 27% YoY to ₹416 cr on revenue of ₹2,442 cr, and implied quarterly PAT has climbed from about ₹359 cr in Q4 FY26 to ₹382 cr and then ₹416 cr; revenue growth accelerated from +16.5% in 9M FY26 to +24.2% in H1 FY27 (no Q2-only YoY is available), net interest revenue grew 31%, gross NPA improved from 2.17% to 1.91% to 1.44%, and PAT margin was flat at about 17% (I disregard the 46.9% FY26 margin and the +49.4% H1 PAT growth as likely extraction errors, and the 1.85% NIM looks non-annualised, so the NIM trend is unconfirmed). The biggest risk is that loans (+26%) are outgrowing deposits (+21%) with a loan-to-deposit ratio near 93%, which could squeeze funding costs and hide credit stress in a fast-growing, unseasoned book.

fundamental.thesis: Karur Vysya Bank is a well-run, Tamil Nadu-based mid-size private bank that has become one of the most profitable lenders in its peer group, with ROE of 20.5% and ROA of 2.1% in Q2FY27. Q2FY27 PAT rose 37.3% YoY to a record Rs 788 cr and advances grew 20.4% YoY. The key bank metrics are moving the right way: NIM has widened every period, from 3.82% (H1FY26) to 4.03%, 4.18% and now 4.34%. GNPA is down to 0.69%, NNPA is 0.18% and provision coverage is about 96%, and management raised its full-year NIM guidance to above 4%. Judged on the bank yardstick (price-to-book against return on equity, not P/E), a P/B of 2.24x for a sustained 19-20% ROE is fair rather than cheap, although the 11.4x trailing P/E, 8.2x forward P/E and rising sell-side estimates (+6.6% over 30 days) show growth is not fully priced in. The main watch-point is funding: deposits grew 16.0% against 20.4% loan growth, CASA is low at about 27.5% and drifting, and cost of deposits is high at 5.49% while yields on advances fell 18 bps. Management's 18-20% credit growth guidance therefore depends on paying up for deposits.

fundamental.thesis: Bank of Maharashtra is a government-controlled (73.6%) mid-size public sector bank with a strong low-cost deposit base (FY26 CASA 52.51%), good asset quality (gross NPA down from 1.45% in FY26 to 1.25% in H1 FY27, net NPA 0.12%, coverage about 98.5%) and FY26 loan growth of 21.74%. H1 FY27 revenue rose 18.6% YoY to Rs 18,799 cr and PAT rose 31.1% to Rs 4,160 cr, but standalone Q2 figures were not extracted, and the 'accelerating' signal is unreliable because it compares a half-year with a full-year figure of only Rs 13,664 cr that appears to use a different revenue definition, while management's maintained 18% FY27 credit growth guidance implies slower growth than FY26. Using the P/B + ROE yardstick for lenders rather than P/E, valuation is fair: 2.07x book with a 22.7% ROE is attractive relative to returns but above the under-1.5x cheap threshold, the stock sits at 95.7% of its 52-week range, and the broad-market peer rank is a weak comparison for a bank, although FY-EPS estimates rose 11.3% over 30 days on thin coverage of 4 analysts. The biggest risk is that fast loan growth with an 86.48% advances-to-deposits ratio squeezes margins or weakens credit quality as new loans season, and the latest NIM trend cannot be confirmed because only the FY26 figure of 3.91% is available.

fundamental.thesis: PNB Housing Finance is a mid-sized housing lender with a Rs 94,124 cr loan book, up 8.9% in six months, and it relies on market borrowing for about 81% of its funding because deposits cover only 18.8% of loans. H1 FY27 revenue rose 11.5% to Rs 4,687 cr while PAT rose only 5.3% to Rs 1,174 cr; subtracting Q1 implies Q2 revenue of about Rs 2,435 cr (about +13.7%, up from +9.2% in Q1) and PAT of about Rs 617 cr (about +5.8%, up from +4.8%), so growth is improving rather than decelerating as the trend table says, since that signal rests on a broken 9MFY26 row, but margins are still under pressure. On P/B plus ROE, the right yardstick for a lender, the stock looks cheap but not deeply so at 1.36x book with ROE of 11.6-12.7%, supported by a trailing P/E of 11.4x against the 18-28x NBFC range, though I give little weight to the broad-market peer rank because it has no true housing-finance peers and I disregard the 49% dividend yield as a data error. The biggest risk is that profit keeps lagging revenue as competition squeezes pricing, and confidence is limited because the data shows no management guidance or Q2 NIM, gross NPA of 0.91% has only a 40% provision cushion, and the 10.74% AUM growth figure looks unreliable against 8.9% growth in six months alone.

fundamental.thesis: Firstsource Solutions (FSL) is a mid-cap BPS/digital-services provider servicing Banking, CMT, and Healthcare verticals for global clients, with a growing $1m+ client roster (45 accounts), six consecutive quarters of 4+ large-deal wins, and 11 straight quarters of QoQ revenue growth — the deal pipeline signals reasonable near-term revenue visibility for its scale. Q1FY27 delivered 12.3% constant-currency revenue growth — a sharp deceleration from +24.5% a year ago — while adjusted PAT grew +31.2% YoY to ₹22cr (8.2% margin) and EBIT margin hit 12.4% for a seventh consecutive quarter of expansion; the company maintained FY27 guidance of 10-13% CC growth and 12.25-12.75% EBIT margin despite absorbing a 1-1.5% headwind from a healthcare BPaaS wind-down, a show of confidence in the deal ramp pipeline. fundamental.thesis: LT Foods is a mid-cap rice-led branded food company, tagged FMCG here, and its most recent extracted numbers are for Q1FY27 because the H1FY27 results filed on 2026-10-27 have no figures in the trend table, so the September quarter is unseen. Q1FY27 revenue rose 26.0% YoY to Rs 3,161 cr while PAT rose only 9.0% to Rs 183 cr (5.8% margin), and FY26 showed the same gap with revenue up 26.1% but PAT up just 2.2%; growth has actually held at about 24-26% and the PAT margin slipped modestly from 6.1% (9MFY26) to 5.8%, because the flagged 'decelerating' and 'contracting' signals are distorted by an implausible Q2FY26 row (Rs 277 cr revenue, 59.1% margin) that I excluded, while Q1FY27 volume growth of 12% with 11% price/mix is good but above the 10% level the sector card treats sceptically, gross margin fell from 34.4% to 32.6%, and FY26 cash conversion was solid (CFO/PAT 1.46x, FCF Rs 551 cr). Using P/E against FMCG norms plus EV/EBITDA as the yardstick, valuation grades cheap at 21.5x trailing P/E versus the 40-65x FMCG norm and 10.4x EV/EBITDA (P11, about 55% below the median), though the peer set is the broad market rather than true industry peers, a low multiple in FMCG can signal a structural issue, the 13.3x forward P/E rests on thin coverage of one analyst, and I disregarded the 105% dividend yield and 28.49 debt/equity as likely data errors and the 7.53x P/B because it does not reconcile with the P/E and 14.9% ROE. The biggest risk is that fast sales growth keeps failing to reach profit, a concern reinforced by the 5.5% cut to FY EPS estimates over the last 30 days and the unverified September quarter.

fundamental.thesis: Castrol India is the market-leading branded lubricants company, with a 167,000-outlet distribution network that grew its rural reach to 46,000 outlets, so it behaves more like a consumer-brands business than the oil PSUs in the Energy sector card. For 9M CY26, revenue rose 20.3% YoY to ₹5,151 cr but PAT grew only 8.7% to ₹766 cr; backing out H1 (₹3,417 cr revenue, ₹590 cr PAT) implies the Sep-quarter revenue grew about 27% to roughly ₹1,734 cr while PAT fell about 22% to roughly ₹176 cr, so PAT margin dropped from 18.6% in the Jun quarter to about 10%, and the implied EBITDA margin of about 15% sits well below management's 21-24% target band. Using EV/EBITDA and P/E as the yardstick (not the PSU 'policy-priced' P/E-plus-yield framework), the stock trades at 17.7x trailing P/E and 11.9x EV/EBITDA, about 50% below the broad-market median (P18/P17), but trailing earnings include the stronger H1 and FY-EPS estimates were cut 4.9% over 30 days, so I grade it fair rather than cheap until margins stabilise. The biggest risk is that crude above $100 and a rupee at 95 per dollar keep raising base-oil costs faster than the company's low double-digit price hikes can pass them through, while weak cash conversion (CFO/PAT 0.52x in H1) suggests working capital is soaking up the growth.

fundamental.thesis: ACME Solar is a renewable power producer with about 2,990 MW running and roughly 5,080 MW under construction, most of it solar, hybrid, firm-and-dispatchable (FDRE) and battery storage (BESS) projects. About 84% of its portfolio sells to central-government buyers on 25-year power purchase agreements (PPAs), and it signed a new 400 MW FDRE PPA with NTPC on 30 Oct. Growth is speeding up: revenue rose from +59% in FY26 to +63% in Q1 FY27 and +78% in H1 FY27, reaching ₹1,745 cr, while H1 PAT more than doubled (+105%) to ₹504 cr and PAT margin widened from 19.9% to 28.9%. Implied Q2 revenue was about ₹791 cr against ₹954 cr in Q1, which fits a weaker monsoon quarter for solar, so H1 is the cleaner read. I valued it on EV/EBITDA, the right measure for a capital-heavy power producer. At 15.2x it sits around the 26th percentile of the broad market, and forward P/E of 13.7x versus trailing 40.7x shows strong earnings growth is already expected. On the other side, P/B of 4.0x with ROE of 10.4% is rich, and the stock is at 80% of its 52-week range, so I call it fair, not cheap. The biggest risk is the balance sheet: debt is about 3.9x equity, interest costs take about 40% of EBITDA, H1 free cash flow was negative ₹5,263 cr from heavy capex, and grid connection delays (about 6 months on average) could push back commissioning and the earnings it depends on.

MRPL is an ONGC-controlled standalone refiner on the west coast, with a small but growing retail fuel network. Its earnings depend mainly on refining margins (GRM), throughput and crude freight costs, not on administered retail prices. Q2 FY27 PAT was ₹1,881 cr, up 194% from ₹639 cr a year ago. Q2 revenue is about ₹35,590 cr (H1 ₹77,199 cr minus Q1 ₹41,609 cr), so the quarter's PAT margin was about 5.3%, up from 2.5% in Q1 and 1.8% for FY26, on an implied GRM near $14.9/bbl and 4.18 MMT throughput. But this comes from a cyclical margin spike, not steady growth. EBITDA margin is still below the 9.5% of Q3 FY26, and the H1 figures don't agree across sources (H1 PAT shows as ₹2,846 cr, ₹2,796 cr, or the ₹2,827 cr sum of the two quarters). On valuation I used EV/EBITDA, as the sector card advises for capital-intensive refiners. At 5.97x EV/EBITDA and 14.5x trailing P/E it looks cheap against the broad market (P3 on EV/EBITDA), but that comparison isn't fair for a commodity refiner. Against refining and PSU energy norms (P/E 6–10x, called policy-priced) it is fair at best. The 3.4x forward P/E is not believable while analysts have cut next-year EPS estimates by 21% in the last 30 days. The biggest risk is GRM falling back from peak levels just as costs stay high: freight is elevated at $7–10/bbl, the Coker Hydrotreater unit is down after its fire until mid-December, and debt/equity is about 1.08x.

fundamental.thesis: DLF is NCR's leading luxury housing developer, and it also earns rental income through its DCCDL office and retail arm, which brings in about ₹6,800 cr a year. Because property sales are booked as revenue only on completion, I judged it on operating numbers rather than P&L: Q2FY27 pre-sales were ₹3,800 cr, below the FY26 run-rate of about ₹5,000 cr a quarter (₹20,143 cr for the year), while reported revenue was ₹2,298 cr and PAT ₹1,301 cr (+11% YoY, 56.6% margin, lifted by the JV share and other income). The 'expanding margin' signal mixes quarterly, half-year and full-year periods, so I don't treat it as a real trend; the stronger evidence is cash from operations at 1.43x PAT and a net cash balance of ₹9,300–15,000 cr (the filings disagree) even after a ₹1,980 cr dividend. For valuation I used the sector yardstick (pre-sales, net cash and the rental annuity) instead of P/E or EV/EBITDA, since both are distorted by the revenue lag; at a ₹1.4L cr market cap, P/B of 3.2x with 10% ROE, and the stock at 23.5% of its 52-week range, I grade it fair. The main risk is that this quarter's soft bookings continue if the Mumbai, Magnolias 2 and Hamilton launches slip, as analysts have already cut FY EPS estimates by 4.8% over 90 days while 20 of 22 still rate it a buy.

fundamental.thesis: Vedanta is a diversified natural-resources producer (aluminium, zinc, oil & gas, iron ore, power) that sells at global commodity prices, so it is judged on its cost position and balance sheet. Its continuing operations shrank after the demerger: H1 FY27 revenue was ₹59,872 cr, down 22.9% YoY, and Q2 revenue fell to ₹26,356 cr from ₹33,515 cr in Q1. Profit is improving even though sales are shrinking: H1 PAT rose 83% YoY to ₹9,123 cr, but Q2 PAT of ₹3,650 cr was below Q1's ₹5,473 cr, with PAT margin slipping from 16.4% to 13.8%. Prior periods were restated for the demerger, so the YoY comparisons are not clean. Using EV/EBITDA as the yardstick, as the sector card advises for commodity names, the stock is cheap: 5.71x is the lowest of 16 Materials peers (sector median 17.9x) and at the low end of the 5–8x mid-cycle band. Forward P/E of 12.7x vs trailing 17.75x, and analysts raising FY EPS estimates by 25% over 90 days, point the same way. The main risks are that Q2 revenue and profit both fell from Q1, and that several data points don't reconcile (yfinance Q2 revenue ₹11,229 cr vs ₹26,356 cr in the filing, a 1038% dividend yield, and a 52-week range distorted by the demerger), so the inputs carry real uncertainty.

Oil India is a government-owned (PSU) upstream oil and gas producer, and it also owns most of the Numaligarh refinery (NRL) through its consolidated accounts. Its earnings mostly track crude prices, production volumes and government policy such as windfall taxes. The latest results are hard to read because the extracted figures mix standalone and consolidated numbers: the H1FY27 table shows revenue of ₹11,915 cr (-33.5% YoY) and PAT of ₹2,520 cr (-31.7%), yet both are lower than the Q1FY27 figures alone (revenue ₹12,886 cr, PAT ₹4,027 cr), so neither set can be trusted as-is. The cleaner signal comes from the company's own press release, which reports a 20% rise in crude production and 116% growth in standalone Q2 PAT (about ₹2,309 cr against roughly ₹1,044 cr a year ago). Cash generation also looks strong, with H1 operating cash flow of ₹8,756 cr, about 3.5 times reported PAT, and analysts raised FY EPS estimates by 11.9% over the last 30 days. On valuation (graded mainly on EV/EBITDA and P/E plus dividend yield, as the sector card advises for PSU upstream), the stock trades at 10.3x trailing P/E, 6.9x forward P/E, 8.3x EV/EBITDA and 1.18x book value with a 12.7% ROE; that is the middle of the 8–14x energy range and the top of the 6–10x PSU-upstream norm, and it sits only about 25% of the way up its 52-week range. That makes it look cheap against the broad market, but the discount reflects permanent policy risk, so we grade it fair rather than cheap. The biggest risks are policy and legal: windfall-tax caps if crude stays near $88, about ₹7,770 cr of disputed GST-on-royalty and Assam land-tax demands, and net debt of about ₹28,800 cr.

fundamental.thesis: United Breweries is India's largest beer maker, owning Kingfisher and selling Heineken, with growth increasingly led by premium brands. Revenue growth improved from +10.0% in Q1 FY27 to +23.7% in Q2 FY27 (₹4,623 cr), with volumes up 16% and premium volumes up 38%, while PAT rose 190.9% to ₹135 cr from a low base of about ₹46 cr after falling 9.6% in Q1; however, the 'accelerating' and 'expanding' trajectory signals are unreliable because they mix quarterly and full-year figures, and the 5.3% PAT margin appears to use net sales (about 2.9% on the listed gross revenue), against about 2.4% on the FY26 gross basis. Using the FMCG card's 40-65x P/E norm, with EV/EBITDA as a cross-check, the stock looks expensive: trailing P/E of 84.0x is above the range and at P92 among peers, EV/EBITDA of 47.9x is at P83, and forward P/E of 46.3x is within the range but implies roughly 82% EPS growth, although the price near its 52-week low (2.6% of range) offers some sentiment support. The biggest risk is that this low-base rebound fades before earnings grow into the valuation, with next-year EPS estimates already cut 8.8% over 90 days and the ₹751.83 cr CCI penalty still before the Supreme Court; the 80% dividend yield and consensus upside figure appear to be data errors and were ignored, and the 29.08 debt/equity is likely a percentage (about 0.29x) but is unverified.

fundamental.thesis: Godrej Consumer Products is India's largest home and personal care company, commanding leadership in household insecticides (Goodknight), hair colour (Godrej Expert), and liquid detergents, with material EM exposure across Africa, Indonesia, and Latin America that amplifies both growth and FX risk. Q4FY26 (latest official quarter) showed revenue of ₹3,885 cr (+11.0% YoY, recovering sharply from +4.0% in Q2FY26) with PAT of ₹452 cr (+10.0% YoY), and volume growth accelerating to 8% from 3% two quarters prior — a genuine demand signal — though full-year FY26 PAT was up just +0.5% on +8.5% revenue growth, reflecting margin headwinds that only partially normalised by year-end. At trailing P/E of 54.9× the stock sits within the 40–65× FMCG sector card range but at P80 vs household-and-personal-care peers (+25% premium to sector median), making it expensive on peer-relative terms; however, forward P/E of 36.3× (vs trailing) signals meaningful earnings recovery is priced in, and the stock trading near its 52-week low (7.8% of range) provides modestly better entry optics than the headline multiple suggests. The biggest risk is the combination of elevated reported debt/equity (34.9) with active Argentina-hyperinflation drag (₹13.5 cr profit headwind cited in Q1FY27 exceptional items) and consistent downward EPS estimate revisions (-1.6% over 90 days), which could cap re-rating even if the domestic volume recovery continues.

trader.reasoning: The analysts don't agree enough to justify a new position, so this is a hold with no buy. fundamental.thesis: UCO Bank is a mid-sized, government-owned lender with gross advances of ₹2,87,690 cr. Its loan book is growing faster each quarter (+16.6% YoY in Q2FY26, +21.2% in Q1FY27, +24.7% in Q2FY27). Q2FY27 net profit rose 26.8% YoY to ₹786 cr, up from +8.1% growth in Q1FY27, and asset quality kept improving: gross NPA fell from 2.56% to 1.96% and net NPA from 0.43% to 0.18% over four quarters, with provision coverage at 98.4%. Net interest income (NII) of ₹2,886 cr is about 13.9% above the year-ago revenue line of ₹2,533 cr, but that row may not be strictly NII, so treat the growth figure as approximate. For a bank we judge value on price-to-book (P/B) against return on equity (ROE), not P/E. P/B of 1.05x is cheap against the market and peers, but ROE is only 8.6% and return on assets 0.8%, well below the 12% ROE needed to call it cheap, so we grade it fair; the 12.7x trailing P/E against a 20.0x forward P/E also suggests the market expects earnings to fall. The biggest risk is funding: loans are growing about 25% while CASA (current and savings account) deposits grow only 10.6%. As a result, the CASA ratio slid from 38.65% to 36.77% and the credit-to-deposit ratio jumped from 75.5% to 82.3%. That pressures margins as the bank pays more for deposits, and it comes in a risk-off market where foreign investors are selling financials.

The executed order book is only about 1x TTM revenue, and Q1 inflows of ₹117 cr are a slow start against management's ₹1,500-2,000 cr FY27 inflow guidance. fundamental.thesis: Engineers India is a state-owned engineering consultancy and turnkey contractor for hydrocarbon, refinery and petrochemical projects, so its revenue comes from working through its order book. H1FY27 revenue fell 8.2% YoY to ₹1,644 cr, and the implied Q2 figure (about ₹824 cr, H1 minus Q1) is down roughly 10% YoY, after +36% to +45% growth in FY26. That makes revenue a clear deceleration story: Turnkey revenue collapsed 46.7%, while the higher-margin Consultancy segment grew 32.9%. That mix shift lifted H1 PAT 138% to ₹355 cr, PAT margin from 8.3% to 21.6% and EBITDA margin to 28.4%. Cash conversion was strong at 1.76x CFO/PAT. Using EV/EBITDA, the Industrials sector card's preferred measure for order-book businesses, the stock trades at 16.75x against a market median of 23.3x (P30), and trailing P/E is 20.6x against the 28–45x Industrials range, so it looks cheap. But it sits at 87% of its 52-week range, and next-FY earnings estimates were cut 8.1% over 90 days, which tempers the upside. The biggest risk is that the margin jump depends on mix (shrinking low-margin turnkey work) and possibly other income, and no order-inflow or order-book figure was given to show that revenue can grow again.

fundamental.thesis: KEI Industries makes wires, cables and EHV power cables, sells increasingly through dealers (58.79% of sales vs 54.12% a year ago), and has a Rs 5,185 cr order book that covers only about 0.34x annualised Q2 revenue, so visibility depends more on channel demand than on the order book. Revenue growth accelerated from +23.0% in Q1FY27 to +38.5% in Q2FY27 (Rs 3,777 cr, with domestic wires and cables up 45.76%), and management raised FY27 growth guidance to 25%+ from 20%, but profit lagged: PAT rose only +29.0% to Rs 262 cr, down from Rs 274 cr in Q1, while PAT margin fell from 8.6% to 7.0% and EBITDA margin from 13.0% to 10.6%, below the roughly 11% guided for FY27. Using EV/EBITDA as the main yardstick, the stock looks expensive at 40.9x (P83 and 75% above the broad-market median, as no tight peer set is available), with trailing P/E of 58.7x above the 28-45x sector range and the price at 97.5% of its 52-week range; the listed +25% consensus upside looks wrong, because the Rs 53,828 cr market cap implies a price near Rs 5,630, which is above the Rs 5,098 mean target. The biggest risk is that a stock priced for perfection de-rates if margins stay under pressure while growth is chased and Sanand capex of about Rs 600 cr a year continues, with FY-EPS estimates already cut 2.5% over the last 30 days; the snapshot's 3.8 debt/equity and 8.0% dividend yield look like data-scale errors and were not relied on.

3M India is the listed Indian arm of 3M, selling diversified products across four segments: Safety & Industrial, Transportation & Electronics, Healthcare and Consumer. It sells catalogue products rather than working through an order book, so the sector card's order-book yardstick does not fit, and I graded it on EV/EBITDA and P/E. In the latest quarter we have extracted figures for (Q1 FY27), revenue grew 19.0% to ₹1,423 cr and PAT grew 31.1% to ₹233 cr (16.4% PAT margin). Revenue growth has picked up from +12.7% in Q3 FY26 and has been double-digit for 5 quarters in a row, led by Healthcare (+23.5%) and Safety & Industrial (+23.0%). Two caveats: EBITDA margin slipped to 17.6% from about 20% in FY26, and the Q3 FY26 loss of ₹62 cr looks like a one-off item, not a fall in the core business. Q2 FY27 results were filed on 6 Nov but are missing from the trend table. Valuation is expensive on our yardstick: trailing P/E is 64.1x against an Industrials range of 28-45x, EV/EBITDA is 36.5x against a market median of 23.3x (77th percentile), and P/B is 20.9x (96th percentile). The forward P/E of 42.2x shows strong earnings growth is already priced in. The biggest risk is that analysts cut FY earnings estimates by 6.5% in the last 30 days, right after the Q2 results we have not seen, which suggests a weak quarter at a premium multiple. That is a classic setup for the stock to re-rate lower.

fundamental.thesis: Reliance is India's largest conglomerate and should be read as four businesses: refining and petrochemicals (O2C), Jio telecom (JPL, now separately listed after its 28 Oct 2026 IPO), retail (RRVL) and a new-energy build-out. Q2FY27 revenue rose 27.8% YoY to ₹362,268 cr, up from +24.5% in Q1 and -8.5% in FY26, and PAT rose 33.8% to ₹29,550 cr, a margin of 8.2% (up from 6.8% in Q1, roughly flat against FY26's 8.3%). Most of that came from O2C, where EBITDA jumped 67.9% to ₹25,203 cr on fuel cracks 3–3.7x higher after Middle East supply disruptions; Jio grew steadily (revenue +11.4%, ARPU ₹218.8), but retail PAT fell 24.3% and JioStar PAT fell 13.2%. Using a sum-of-the-parts view with EV/EBITDA as the main multiple, the stock trades at 12.2x EV/EBITDA and 21.7x trailing / 18.0x forward P/E; that looks expensive against the PSU energy median (9.2x P/E), but that comparison is misleading for a conglomerate earning telecom and retail multiples, so I grade it fair. It trades near its 52-week low, has strong cash conversion (CFO/PAT 1.76x) and modest leverage (net debt/EBITDA 0.47x). The biggest risk is that the record quarter depends on crack spreads created by a geopolitical shock, which can reverse quickly while retail and media are weakening.

fundamental.thesis: HDFC Bank is India's largest private-sector bank, with ₹33.2L cr of deposits, ₹33.2L cr of advances and 9,706 branches, and its asset quality is very clean: GNPA is 1.11%, down from 1.15% at FY26-end, net NPA is 0.37% and credit cost is 44 bps. On volume, Q2FY27 deposits grew +18.8% YoY and advances grew +16.3%, but profitability is moving the wrong way. Management calls the 3.32% NIM a cycle low, ROA has fallen from 1.9% in FY26 to 1.48% in H1FY27, and H1 PAT of ₹35,869 cr is down -10.2% YoY on revenue down -4.1%, a 14.3% PAT margin. The ₹1,950 cr Q2 PAT figure (+12.7%) looks like an extraction error, and 30-day and 90-day FY EPS estimates have both been cut 5.6%. Using the lender yardstick of P/B against ROE, 1.98x book on a 13.8% TTM ROE (12.1% in H1) is fair in absolute terms, but it ranks P79 among bank peers on P/B even though P/E sits at the peer median of 16.8x. The stock is at 8.6% of its 52-week range, which helps the entry but does not make it cheap. The biggest risk is an abrupt leadership change: a new MD/CEO effective immediately and the Deputy MD retiring by December. This comes with a loan-to-deposit ratio near 100%, LCR tight at 113%, and a 25 bps October rate hike that management expects to reprice the 70% floating book upward, which conflicts with the sector card's easing-cycle prior.

fundamental.thesis: Bharti Airtel is the number-two player in India's mobile market, which is now effectively a 2.5-player market, and it leads on premium customers, with growing broadband, enterprise and Africa businesses on top. In Q2 FY27 mobile ARPU (average revenue per user) reached Rs 271, up 5.9% YoY and up from Rs 257 in Q4 FY26, and data usage per customer grew 28.8%. The extracted Q2 row shows revenue up 16.7% YoY and PAT up 30.8%, with a 14.6% PAT margin and a 57.9% EBITDA margin. However, the absolute figures in that row (Rs 6,088 cr revenue against Rs 21,097 cr in Q4 FY26 and about Rs 2.11L cr for FY26) are clearly not on a like-for-like consolidated basis, so the pre-computed 'decelerating/contracting' trajectory signals are unreliable and I have not relied on them. I graded valuation on the sector card's yardstick, EV/EBITDA: at 10.54x it sits inside the 9-12x norm for Indian mobile, so it is fair. Forward P/E of 21.6x against trailing 40.7x shows earnings growth is expected, and the stock is at only 15% of its 52-week range, which makes the entry better on risk/reward. The biggest risk is that without a fresh round of industry-wide tariff hikes, ARPU growth of about 6% falls short of the ~Rs 300 target that today's valuation and the slight downward EPS revisions (-0.6% over 90 days) are watching.

fundamental.thesis: Coal India is the state-controlled near-monopoly coal miner that supplies most of India's thermal power fuel, and it earns a steady return from domestic volumes, e-auction premiums and a high dividend payout. In H1 FY27 revenue rose +13.8% YoY to ₹90,434 cr and PAT rose +18.9% to ₹15,397 cr (PAT margin 17.0%), recovering from a weak FY26 (revenue -0.5%, PAT -12.3%). The quality of that growth is mixed: offtake rose +7.6% to 384.2 MT while production fell -2% to 321 MT, so part of the growth came from selling down inventory, which fell 49% to 130.3 MT. Cash conversion was strong (CFO/PAT 2.21x, FCF ₹26,270 cr). I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA plus P/E and yield, as the sector card prescribes for PSU energy names. At 6.1x EV/EBITDA and 9.2x trailing P/E the stock sits exactly at the Energy peer median (P50) and inside the 6–10x policy-priced band, so it is fair, not cheap. The stock is at 85% of its 52-week range and EPS estimates are drifting slightly lower (-0.9% over 30d), which limits upside. The main risk is that volume growth cannot continue once the inventory buffer is used up while production is still falling, and administered pricing caps any offset from price.

fundamental.thesis: Wipro is India's fourth-largest IT services exporter and lags tier-1 peers on growth; the sector is in an AI-driven reset where legacy time-and-materials revenue is shrinking. H1FY27 revenue rose 9.8% YoY to ₹49,231 cr, a sharp pickup from near-flat FY26 (Q4FY26 at -0.2%), but PAT slipped 0.7% to ₹6,556 cr and PAT margin has compressed from 14.7% to 13.3% over the trend window. The revenue pickup probably owes part of its size to the Mindsprint acquisition and a weak rupee rather than real organic demand, and several trend rows look inconsistent, so the figures are unreliable. Using trailing P/E and EV/EBITDA as the yardsticks, Wipro is cheap: 15.6x P/E against a 22–30x sector band and a 24.7x peer median, and 10.5x EV/EBITDA, the lowest among its 8 peers. fundamental.thesis: JSW Steel is a large Indian steelmaker that sold a record 7.46 MT in Q2FY27 (+13% YoY), with auto-sector sales up 36%. Revenue growth accelerated from +9.8% in Q1 to +20.6% (₹54,486 cr), and PAT rose 225.6% to ₹5,359 cr, though the YoY figures use a low, restructured base; PAT margin was flat at about 9.8-9.9%, the 'contracting' signal is distorted by FY26's ₹18,051 cr one-off gain, and EBITDA per tonne fell about 11% QoQ from ₹14,990 to ₹13,329 despite rising 24% YoY. On EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a steel cyclical, the stock is expensive: the reported 12.6x, or roughly 9x on my estimate using annualised Q2 EBITDA and net debt, is above the 5-8x mid-cycle norm, and the 13.8x trailing P/E and 'cheap vs peers' verdict carry little weight because of the one-off gain and a peer set that includes paint and adhesive companies. The biggest risk is that steel spreads narrow from here, with the stock at 92% of its 52-week range and EBITDA per tonne already falling sequentially, leaving little room for error.

Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles is the demerged passenger-car business. It owns Jaguar Land Rover (JLR), which brings in most of its revenue, plus the domestic Tata PV/EV franchise, a market leader in Indian EVs with an EV mix of about 14% in FY26. In Q2FY27 revenue rose 33.9% YoY to ₹96,920 cr, up from +9.3% in Q1FY27, but that jump mostly comes from an easy comparison: JLR's cyber-incident quarter (Q3FY26 revenue was -25.8%). Revenue barely moved from last quarter (₹95,799 cr to ₹96,920 cr), EBITDA margin fell from 7.4% to 5.5%, and PAT went from +₹859 cr to a ₹5,451 cr loss (-5.6% margin) after ₹6,738 cr of one-off restructuring charges (₹3,776 cr staff separation plus ₹2,856 cr impairment). Strip out those charges and the business still barely broke even, with an EBIT margin of about 0.4–1.1%. On EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-heavy carmaker, the stock trades at 7.1x versus an Indian auto peer median of 18.3x, with P/B at 1.3x and forward P/E at 7.2x, all the cheapest in the sector. We grade it 'fair', not 'cheap', because the comparison set is Indian volume makers, while a JLR-heavy business should trade nearer global luxury-car multiples. ROE is negative, and analysts have cut this year's EPS estimates by 35% in 30 days, so the low multiple largely reflects falling earnings, not mispricing. The biggest risk is JLR margins getting squeezed by rising commodity costs and a weaker product mix while capex runs at about 21% of revenue, which pushes free cash flow negative and net debt up to ₹50.8K cr.

fundamental.thesis: Tata Steel is one of India's largest integrated steelmakers, and its profits come mostly from the high-margin India business, which posted an EBITDA margin of about 25% in Q2FY27; the loss-making European plants in the Netherlands (TSN) and the UK (TSUK) pull the group numbers down. In Q2FY27 consolidated revenue was ₹65,436 cr, up 11.5% YoY, and PAT was ₹3,700 cr, up 16.3% YoY, for a PAT margin of 5.7%. The pre-computed signal calls revenue growth 'accelerating', but it actually slowed from +14.3% in Q1. Group EBITDA margin improved from 15.4% to 16.3% and EBITDA per tonne rose from ₹12,898 to ₹13,462, but the India EBITDA margin slipped from 26.8% to 25.0%. Part of the reported PAT may be the ₹3,457 cr one-off accounting gain from the TMILL stake revaluation (Aug 2026), so the underlying profit quality is unclear. Management expects a stronger H2: India realisations up ₹3,500–3,600/t in Q3, ₹7,000 cr of cost savings targeted for FY27 (₹1,800 cr delivered so far), and a UK breakeven in Q4. Analysts have raised FY EPS estimates by about 5% and next-FY estimates by about 9%. On valuation I used EV/EBITDA, the right measure for a capital-intensive steelmaker. At 10.4× it sits at P13 among Materials peers, but that peer group is skewed by paint companies and looks rich against the 5–8× mid-cycle range for steel. The forward P/E of 10.8× against a trailing 23.5× already prices in strong earnings growth, and other steel names (JSWSTEEL, JINDALSTEL, HINDALCO) are cheaper, so I grade it fair, not cheap. The biggest risk is the Netherlands unit: regulators may revoke key plant permits, it is flagged as a going concern with material uncertainty, there is a large unrecognised impairment risk, and the auditor has issued a modified opinion. Net debt of ₹91,423 cr (2.4× EBITDA) adds to that risk.

fundamental.thesis: IndusInd Bank is a mid-sized private lender, heavy on vehicle finance (28% of loans, 58% retail), that is still rebuilding after the FY26 accounting-discrepancy year in which full-year PAT fell 65% to ₹891 cr and ROA dropped to 0.17%. Per the H1FY27 filing, total income rose 26.8% YoY to ₹23,873 cr and PAT rose 36.4% to ₹2,279 cr, but this flatters the core business: the comparison base includes a Q2FY26 loss, Q1FY27 includes a one-off ₹868 cr IFR transfer, and operating profit actually fell 7.9% YoY to ₹10,323 cr. Loan growth has recovered from -8.5% (FY26) to +11% YoY, but NIM has slipped to 3.23% from 3.39–3.48%, credit cost is elevated at 1.4%, cost-to-income is high at 57.9%, and annualised Q2 ROE is only 7.4%. Using the bank yardstick (P/B with ROE, ignoring the distorted 80× trailing P/E), a P/B of 1.08× (P29 vs peers, 26% below the 1.5× median) fits sub-par returns of about 7% ROE, so the valuation is fair rather than cheap; the cheap case only holds if ROE recovers toward 12%+. The biggest risk is that the earnings recovery stalls as NIM compression and above-normal vehicle and microfinance credit costs hold ROA under 1%.

fundamental.thesis: Apollo Hospitals is India's largest private hospital chain (about 8,500 operating beds), with a pharmacy and digital-health arm (AHLL / Apollo 24/7) that adds scale. Consolidated revenue growth has accelerated over the four clean quarters, from +13% in Q2FY26 to +17%, +21% and now +23% YoY at Rs 7,615 cr in Q2FY27. PAT rose 32% to Rs 630 cr and PAT margin widened from 7.6% to 8.3%, backed by occupancy rising to 73% from 69%, inpatient volumes up 14% and ARPP up 8%. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-heavy hospital operator: at 33.5x it is 44% above the sector median of 23.3x (P75), with trailing P/E of 61.8x and forward P/E of 39.1x, and the stock sits at 87% of its 52-week range, so it is expensive even after allowing for the strong growth. The biggest risk is that 1,280 new beds (Rs 35 cr EBITDA loss this quarter) ramp slower than planned while the hospitals CEO exits, which would dent margins at a valuation that leaves little room for a miss.

Eicher Motors owns Royal Enfield, which holds about 87% of India's mid-size premium motorcycle market, and also owns 50% of the VECV commercial-vehicle joint venture. That makes it a direct beneficiary of the premiumisation trend in two-wheelers. For H1 FY27, revenue grew 25.3% YoY to ₹14,054 cr and PAT grew 17.9% to ₹3,036 cr. Subtracting Q1 from H1 gives Q2 FY27 revenue of about ₹7,422 cr (+20.3% YoY) and PAT of about ₹1,573 cr (+14.9% YoY), so growth has slowed from +31.6% in Q1, PAT is growing more slowly than revenue, and PAT margin has slipped from 23.6% in FY26 to about 21.2%. Using the OEM P/E and EV/EBITDA yardstick from the sector card, the stock is expensive: trailing P/E of 37.9x is above the 18-30x OEM range and the 27.1x peer median (P80), and EV/EBITDA of 33.7x and P/B of 8.3x are both the highest among peers (P100). Forward P/E of 28.8x and analyst estimates edging up (+1% over 30 days) partly support the premium, but with the stock at 79% of its 52-week range there is limited room for upside. The main risk is that slowing revenue growth and shrinking PAT margins, possibly from input-cost inflation and mix, cause this premium valuation to fall.

fundamental.thesis: Grasim is an Aditya Birla holding company and operating business: it controls UltraTech (India's largest cement maker, now 210 mtpa), Aditya Birla Capital and a renewables arm, and it directly runs cellulosic fibre (VSF), chemicals, Birla Opus paints and the Birla Pivot B2B e-commerce business. In Q2 FY27, consolidated revenue rose 26.0% YoY to ₹50,105 cr, helped by cement volumes (+12.9%), lending book growth (+32%), Birla Opus (+35%) and Birla Pivot (+66%). Profit to shareholders, however, swung to a ₹234 cr loss from ₹3,846 cr in Q1. Two things drove that: a ₹767 cr exceptional charge for idling the Canadian pulp mill (AVNB), and EBITDA margin falling from 23.5% to 13.0%. H1 PAT is up a more modest 12.2% on 23.5% revenue growth. Because this is a capital-intensive conglomerate, I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA and P/B, not trailing P/E (42.4×, P73, inflated by depressed owner profit). EV/EBITDA of 13.2× (P27, 26% below the Materials median of 17.9×) and P/B of 2.1× (P19) look cheap, but a normal holding-company discount and an ROE of only 6.3% offset that. Forward P/E of 21.2× sits right at the peer median, so overall it is fair, with the stock already at 87% of its 52-week range. fundamental.thesis: KPIT Technologies is a mid-cap software engineering specialist for global carmakers, focused on vehicle features, middleware and connected services, and it depends heavily on its strategic clients (84.6% of Q4 FY26 revenue). Q2 FY27 revenue rose 6.5% YoY to Rs 1,691 cr, with growth slowing from +12.0% in Q4 FY26 (the table's Rs 17,110 cr for Q4 is a units error; about Rs 1,711 cr reconciles to FY26), while PAT fell 28.6% to Rs 121 cr and PAT margin slipped from 9.5% in Q4 to 7.1%, although EBITDA margin recovered to 17.8% from an implied 14-15% in Q1, and deal wins of USD 213 mn are only about 1.2x quarterly revenue. On trailing P/E, the main yardstick for this asset-light business, valuation is fair at 26.0x, inside the 22-30x sector range and near the 26.9x peer median (P46), and the near-52-week-low price and EV/EBITDA discount (10.8x vs 15.2x) look less compelling because TTM EBITDA of about Rs 1,140 cr implies closer to 12.8x, while the 17.6x forward P/E requires about 48% EPS growth even as FY estimates were cut 10.5% in 30 days; the 23.62 debt/equity and 136% dividend yield appear to be data errors given Rs 507 cr of net cash, so neither was used. The biggest risk is that earnings keep falling as estimates are cut, with weak cash conversion (H1 CFO/PAT 0.50x, FCF Rs 6 cr), so the stock could be a falling knife rather than a value entry.

Mphasis is a mid-sized Indian IT services company with a heavy tilt toward banking and insurance clients. Almost all its revenue (98.6%) comes from direct clients, and it is repositioning around AI-led work through Mphasis.AI and its Tria platform. Growth has picked up: constant-currency revenue growth rose from +7.1% YoY in Q4FY26 to +11.3% in Q2FY27, and PAT grew +19.0% YoY. Management raised its FY27 revenue guidance from high single digits to low double digits, and the deal pipeline hit a record $9.3 Bn, up 23% YoY. That is well ahead of the sector, where tier-1 names are growing near zero. However, operating margin is flat at 14.8%, down from 15.3% a year ago, and cash conversion is weak: FY26 operating cash flow was only 0.67x PAT, and receivable days (DSO) jumped to 113 from 95. On valuation, I used P/E and EV/EBITDA for this asset-light IT business. Trailing P/E of 24.7x sits inside the 22–30x IT sector range and exactly at the peer median (P50). EV/EBITDA is also at the median (14.7x), and P/B of 4.4x is at P25. Forward P/E of 18.3x is below trailing, which means earnings growth is expected, and the stock sits at 30% of its 52-week range. Overall that grades as fair, with a mildly favourable entry point. The biggest risk is that AI-led deals turn out to cannibalise legacy revenue rather than add to it, which would compress margins while the slow cash collection continues.

fundamental.thesis: Alkem is one of India's largest branded-generics makers, about 68% of sales from the domestic market. It ranks No. 1 in trade generics, holds leading positions in anti-infectives and the Semaglutide (GLP-1) market, and has 15 brands ranked in the top 3; it also has smaller US, biotech (Enzene) and MedTech (Occlutech) businesses. In Q2FY27 revenue grew 13.8% YoY to ₹4,552 cr and EBITDA margin was 22.5% (gross margin up 220 bps to 67.2%), but consolidated PAT fell 14.4% YoY to ₹667 cr because of a higher tax rate under the new regime; India sales grew only 9.5%, slower than the 13.8% IQVIA growth figure, and US sales growth slowed sharply from 20.3% in FY26 to 2.4%, with mid-teens price erosion. Valuation looks fair on the P/E-versus-peers yardstick the sector card uses for India-branded franchises: trailing P/E is 27.4x and forward P/E 23.1x, both at P31 among 14 peers and 25% below the 36.4x peer median, while EV/EBITDA of 20.2x is near the median (P46); the stock sits at 46% of its 52-week range, so the discount is real but small. The biggest risks are the August 2026 OAI on the Daman plant and slow-but-steady analyst estimate cuts (FY EPS down 2.4% over 90 days), which could keep earnings flat even as revenue grows. The live data also has errors: dividend yield shows 100%, debt/equity shows 14.27 (most likely meaning 0.14x), the Q3FY26 row is mis-scaled, and the yfinance quarterly rows don't match the filings.

fundamental.thesis: Biocon is India's largest biosimilars company, selling insulins, oncology and immunology biosimilars mainly in North America (~40% of revenue) and Europe (~35%), with a generics arm and a stake in Syngene (CRDMO). Growth has slowed: H1FY27 revenue was Rs 8,725 cr, up 5.9% YoY, after growth of 17.3%, 14.0% and 10.0% in earlier periods. Biosimilars grew 9% and generics 15%, but services fell 12%. EBITDA margin dropped from 22% to 20%, and PAT of Rs 182 cr is only a 2.1% margin because Rs 453 cr of half-year interest absorbs most operating profit. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, because heavy debt makes the P/E misleading. At 23.3x, EV/EBITDA is exactly the sector median (P50), so the grade is fair. The earnings-based multiples look much worse: trailing P/E is 147.6x (the most expensive of 17 Healthcare peers), forward P/E is 35.5x (P69), and a P/B of 2.0x is backed by only 1.1% ROE, so a median multiple is not cheap for a business growing about 6%. The biggest risk is that sell-side FY EPS estimates have been cut about 18% in 30 to 90 days while most ratings stay bullish, a classic pattern before a stock re-rates lower. The H2 pickup management talks about (Pertuzumab launch in Europe, extra Malaysia insulin capacity, Yesafili/Yesintek ramp-up) has no numbers attached.

Using trailing P/E and EV/EBITDA against peers, the stock is expensive: the listed 50.5x P/E appears to use FY26 EPS and is about 43x on my trailing-12-month estimate, still above the 28-40x sector range, while EV/EBITDA of 28.0x is 31% above the peer median (P77); I ignored the implausible 8.0% dividend yield and used net debt of 1.1x EBITDA (FY26) rather than the 38.11 debt/equity flag, which looks like a percentage. fundamental.thesis: Bharat Forge is a global forging and auto-components maker that is shifting toward defence and aerospace. Its overseas auto operations in Germany (BF CDP) and the US are struggling, with EBITDA margins of about 3.5–4%. H1 FY27 consolidated revenue grew 19.8% YoY to ₹9,510 cr, up from roughly +7–11% in FY26, helped by defence revenue up about 47%. But PAT fell 67.7% to ₹189 cr (2.0% margin, against about 7.3% a year ago) because of large exceptional charges, mainly the restructuring provision for the German unit. Backing out Q1, the Sep quarter alone made about ₹279 cr of PAT on about ₹4,870 cr of revenue (around 5.7% margin), so EBITDA margin of about 15.3% is holding but has slipped from 17.4% in FY26. Because this is a capital-intensive business I graded valuation mainly on EV/EBITDA, and it looks expensive. EV/EBITDA of 33.4x is about 75% above the auto-parts peer median of 19.1x, trailing P/E of 86x and forward P/E of 39.6x are the highest among peers, and P/B of 9.7x is paired with only an 11.6% ROE. The stock is also at 88% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is that the price already assumes a smooth defence ramp and a recovery in Europe and the US, while analysts keep cutting estimates (FY EPS down 11.3% over 90 days) and H1 free cash flow was negative at ₹-616 cr.

MRF is India's largest tyre maker by revenue, with a net cash balance sheet (₹1,850 cr net cash, AAA credit rating) and a strong position in replacement and OEM tyres. Sales are growing but profits are shrinking: H1 FY27 revenue rose 13.4% YoY to ₹17,076 cr while PAT fell 14.3% to ₹882 cr, and the September quarter worked out from the half-year figures was weaker still, with revenue of about ₹8,660 cr (+17.4% YoY) and PAT of about ₹387 cr (-26% YoY). That puts the quarter's EBITDA margin near 10.3%, down from 17.8% in Q3 FY26 and 14.1% in Q1 FY27, because raw materials now take 72.7% of revenue. Using EV/EBITDA as the main yardstick for a capital-heavy business, the stock looks cheap against its auto-parts peers (EV/EBITDA 11.1x vs a 19.1x median, P/E 22.5x vs 39.2x, lowest in the group), but its P/E sits inside the 18-28x range for auto companies, part of the discount is normal for tyre makers (BALKRISIND is also among the cheapest), and analysts have cut FY EPS estimates by 8.3% over 90 days, so we grade it fair, not cheap. The biggest risk is that raw-material costs stay high while inventory jumped 32% since March to ₹7,163 cr and H1 free cash flow turned negative (₹-371 cr, cash flow only 0.72x PAT), so profits could keep falling and the low multiple may not turn out to be cheap. Note that the snapshot's 36% dividend yield and 15.29 debt/equity look like data errors: the filings show debt/equity of 0.03 and net cash, and the ₹3 interim dividend is tiny next to a share price above ₹1.2 lakh.

fundamental.thesis: Thermax is a mid-cap capital-goods company selling boilers, heating, cooling, water and environmental systems, plus a growing green-energy and renewable-utility arm, and it benefits from India's industrial capex cycle. Consolidated revenue growth picked up to +11.4% YoY in Q2FY27 (Rs 2,756 cr), from +6.7% in Q1 and about +3-4% through FY26, but profit has not followed: Q2 PAT fell 5% YoY to Rs 113 cr (4.1% margin vs 4.8% a year ago), Q1 PAT collapsed 85% to Rs 22 cr, and Q2 was propped up by Rs 20 cr of one-off PSI incentive income alongside a Rs 15 cr Green Solutions impairment, so the core margin trend is contracting. Grading on EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for an order-book industrial, the stock trades at 53.5x, 57% above the 34x peer median and at the 82nd percentile, with trailing P/E of 76x well above the 28-45x sector band; that is expensive, especially with the price at about 91% of its 52-week range and sell-side FY EPS estimates cut about 14% over 30-90 days (the quoted +40% upside looks erroneous, since a Rs 3,900 mean target sits below the current price). The biggest risk is that order momentum is fading: consolidated order booking fell 8% YoY to Rs 3,259 cr, the Rs 14,250 cr backlog covers only about 1.3x annual revenue, and free cash flow was negative (FY26 FCF -Rs 411 cr, CFO/PAT 0.75x), which leaves little room for a multiple this rich.

fundamental.thesis: BHEL is India's dominant PSU power equipment and heavy engineering manufacturer, with leading exposure to thermal power, defence, and T&D — a direct beneficiary of the government-led capex upcycle in power and infrastructure. Q2FY27 revenue accelerated to ₹9,300 cr (+23.8% YoY from ₹7,512 cr), PAT surged 118.9% to ₹821 cr (margin 8.8%), confirming a clear multi-period turnaround: PAT margins have expanded from -0.7% in H1FY26 through 4.5%, 4.7%, 4.9%, to 8.8% now, with H1FY27 PAT of ₹1,198 cr vs a ₹80.6 cr loss a year ago. On the primary Industrials yardstick (EV/EBITDA), BHEL trades at 56.2× vs sector median 34.0× — P88 in sector, a 65% premium — and while the forward P/E of 29.7× is a reassuring P35 (below median), the stock is at 82.6% of its 52-week range with ROE of only 6.3% against P/B of 5.15×, graded expensive overall. The most critical data gap is the absence of current order-book and book-to-bill figures, which are the primary leading indicator for any capital-goods name; without these, it is impossible to confirm that the execution ramp is sustainable, and any government capex pause could trigger the 30–50% de-rating this sector is historically prone to from near-highs.

fundamental.thesis: SRF is a diversified Indian chemicals and packaging-films maker; most of its profit comes from refrigerant gases and specialty chemicals for agrochemical and pharma clients. The SECTOR CARD places it in specialty chemicals, with the ref-gas cycle turning up. The latest quarter in the official trend table is Q1FY27, which showed revenue of ₹5,033 cr (+31.8% YoY) and PAT of ₹759 cr (+75.5% YoY), with EBITDA margin rising to 25.2% from about 18-20% through 9MFY26 and FY26 (FY26 revenue grew only +7.5%, so growth has re-accelerated sharply). However, the Q2FY27 results filed on 21 Oct are not yet in the extracted table, the yfinance Q2 revenue of ₹2,600 cr looks inconsistent with that run-rate (likely standalone or partial), and the H1FY26 row appears mislabelled, so the newest quarter is unverified. On valuation I used EV/EBITDA, the yardstick the card names for chemical cyclicals: 19.2x EV/EBITDA, 34.6x trailing P/E and 27.9x forward P/E sit well above the card's 5-8x mid-cycle EV/EBITDA and the 12-22x Materials P/E band, so it grades expensive. The 'cheap vs peers' verdict is not usable because the peer set is capital-goods names (ABB, CGPOWER, HAL) after a yfinance Industrials mis-tag; the stock sitting near its 52-week low (19% of range) only partly offsets this. The biggest risk is earnings quality and cycle dependence: H1 cash conversion was weak (CFO/PAT 0.63x, FCF -₹180 cr) during a heavy capex phase (₹974 cr in H1), with ₹165 cr of forex losses, so any cooling in refrigerant-gas pricing would hit a peak-margin earnings base.

fundamental.thesis: Coromandel International is India's second-largest phosphatic fertiliser company, with about 17.5% of the phosphatic market, and it has a growing crop-protection arm after buying 53% of NACL Industries. In Q2FY27 revenue rose 6.6% YoY to ₹10,294 cr, but PAT fell 34.0% YoY to ₹523 cr (5.1% margin). This is the third quarter in a row of falling profit (-80.1% in Q4FY26, -23.9% in Q1FY27, -34.0% now), while revenue growth has slowed from +30.7% to +19.0% to +15.9% to +6.6%. The fertiliser business is subsidy-driven and does not match the sector card's steel/cement/paints yardsticks, so I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA. At 17.3x it is close to the peer median of 17.9x (P47). Trailing P/E is 31.6x, below the peer median of 37.3x but above the 12–22x Materials benchmark, so overall it is fair, not cheap. The bigger warning is earnings estimates: analysts have cut this year's EPS forecast by about 23% in 30 days, yet 8 of 9 still rate it a buy. Profits are also not turning into cash: H1 operating cash flow was only ₹54 cr against ₹1,220 cr of pre-tax profit, as working capital and subsidy receivables absorb cash. Note that the snapshot's 56% dividend yield and 11.47x debt/equity are almost certainly data errors. Filings show net debt of ₹574 cr against ₹14,010 cr of equity, which is low leverage.

PI Industries is an Indian agrochemical company that makes chemicals under contract for global innovator companies and also sells crop-protection products in India, with a smaller pharma arm that is growing. It is also launching its own molecules, such as Pioxaniliprole, announced on 2026-10-29. Business is getting worse: Q2FY27 revenue was ₹1,702 cr (-9.1% YoY) and PAT was ₹122 cr (-70.1% YoY), so PAT margin fell to 7.2% from 13.8% in Q1. H1FY27 PAT fell 54.7% to ₹366 cr and EBITDA fell 43.1%, which makes this the third straight period of falling revenue and shrinking margins, in line with the sector card's warning that Chinese price competition is capping agrochem prices. On valuation I used EV/EBITDA, the yardstick the sector card names for cyclical chemicals: at 22.1×, PIIND trades 23% above the Materials peer median of 17.9× even though its EBITDA is shrinking fast, so I grade it expensive. The trailing P/E of 29.4× (P33 vs peers) looks fair only because it still counts earlier, stronger quarters. The forward P/E of 21.3× assumes a recovery that the latest quarter does not support yet. Being near the 52-week low (4% of range) makes the stock look cheaper but does not help the business case. The biggest risk is that the drop in export contract volumes and margins is structural rather than a passing inventory correction, which would push estimates down further.

fundamental.thesis: Jubilant FoodWorks runs India's largest QSR network: Domino's India, a fast-growing Popeyes, and DP Eurasia (Domino's and Coffy in Turkey), with 3,820 stores across the group. Reported PAT fell 42.7% to ₹111.6 cr (4.3% margin) because Dunkin was moved to discontinued operations. Profit from continuing operations grew only 0.5% to ₹113.9 cr. EBITDA grew 7.3%, slower than revenue, and EBITDA margin fell 83 bps to 19.7%. On the positive side, Domino's India like-for-like sales growth improved from 0.2% to 2.5% to 4.1% over the last three quarters, Popeyes grew revenue 122%, and cash generation is strong (H1 CFO is 4.6x PAT, though lease accounting inflates this ratio). fundamental.thesis: Voltas is India's largest room-AC (RAC) brand, with a 17.4% market share and a 4.2 pp lead over the No. 2 player; RAC volumes grew 32% in Q2 FY27, and its Voltbek appliance venture is also gaining share (washing machines 8.8%, refrigerators 7.0%). That includes a ₹63 cr one-off write-back from the Sidra bank guarantee case and ₹25 cr of PLI incentive income, so the core business was likely close to breakeven or loss-making in Q2. Reported H1 FY27 numbers are weaker: revenue rose 107.8% YoY to ₹2,441 cr, but PAT fell 49.8% to ₹495 cr (12.6% margin). That PAT includes a ₹309 cr non-cash fair-value gain, so underlying profit is roughly ₹186 cr. Operating cash flow was negative at ₹-724 cr, and net debt rose from ₹7,607 cr in Q1 to ₹8,111 cr. The trend table mixes quarterly, half-year and full-year periods, so the 'accelerating' and 'contracting' labels are not reliable, and H1 FY27 bookings and collections are not in the data, which leaves a gap in the metrics that matter most here. I graded valuation on enterprise value to pre-sales (bookings) and P/B against ROE, not P/E, because reported profit here lags actual sales by 2–4 years. Enterprise value is about ₹59,500 cr, or roughly 1.7× FY26 bookings. P/B is 2.68× against ROE of 10%, and the stock sits at 25% of its 52-week range, so it looks fair, leaning slightly cheap. The biggest risk is that cash generation weakens while debt rises in a risk-off market.

P&G Hygiene & Health Care is a debt-free, standalone FMCG company with leading feminine-hygiene (Whisper) and healthcare (Vicks) brands, a 114.9% ROE and strong cash conversion (CFO/PAT 1.16x in H1FY27). Using P/E and EV/EBITDA, it looks cheap: trailing P/E of 35.2x is below the FMCG band of 40–60x and about 20% under the peer median of 43.8x (P0, the cheapest of 6 peers), and EV/EBITDA of 24.8x compares with a peer median of 31.0x. But the sector card warns that 'cheap FMCG' usually signals a structural problem, and here the discount comes with flat sales, falling margins and EPS estimates cut 5.7% over 90 days. The biggest risk is that this is a value trap: no volume-growth figures were disclosed, so we can't tell whether demand is weakening or margins are being hit by input costs or ad spending, and the cheapness case only holds if margins recover.

fundamental.thesis: Petronet LNG runs India's largest LNG import and regasification terminals (Dahej, now expanded to 22.5 MTPA, plus Kochi). It earns mainly on volumes and regas tariffs, so LNG price swings flow through revenue without much effect on profit. In H1 FY27, revenue fell 44.3% YoY to ₹12,760 cr, which mostly reflects lower LNG prices and the Qatar supply disruption, while PAT rose 43.1% to ₹2,394 cr (18.8% margin). Q2 PAT was a record ₹1,235 cr, up 53%, but part of that came from ₹658 cr of 'operational efficiency' gains that may not repeat, and terminal utilisation fell to 64% from 78% a year ago. Cash conversion is solid (CFO/PAT 1.25x, FCF ₹1,294 cr), and full-year EPS estimates have been raised 31% over 90 days. fundamental.thesis: GIC Re is India's dominant state-owned reinsurer. It takes on risk from domestic insurers across fire, motor, health, agriculture and other lines, and AM Best rates it A- (Excellent) with a stable outlook. In H1 FY27, gross written premium grew 11.7% year on year to ₹24,713 cr, faster than the +5.8% to +6.4% of FY26 and H1 FY26. Profit fell the other way: consolidated PAT dropped 12.8% to ₹4,709 cr, PAT margin shrank from 26.8% to 19.1%, and the combined ratio worsened slightly from 106.36% to 106.79%. That means the company loses money on underwriting and relies on ₹5,015 cr of investment income. Q2 alone (about ₹2,966 cr of PAT, implied by H1 minus Q1) was much better than Q1, whose PAT fell 31%. For an insurer I grade value on price-to-book against ROE, not P/E. At 0.62x book, the cheapest in the peer set and near the bottom of its 52-week range, the stock is cheap even for a below-par 9.1% ROE, and the 4.18x solvency ratio gives a large capital buffer. The trailing P/E of 6.8x supports this but is not my yardstick. The ROE gap is the main reason the market keeps this PSU at a discount to book. The biggest risk is that underwriting losses stay above 100% of premium while estimates keep being cut (FY EPS down 10% over 90 days), so earnings would depend on volatile investment gains.

Subtracting Q1 from H1 gives Q2FY27 revenue of about ₹1,502 cr (+47% YoY on a weak, -9.5% base) and PAT of about ₹725 cr (+54%), so growth slowed from +66% in Q1. The 'accelerating' signal relies on a Q4FY26 revenue row (₹147 cr) that doesn't fit the FY26 total, and H1 PAT includes a one-off ₹81 cr gain from the AMC stake sale. fundamental.thesis: HDB Financial Services is a large-scale NBFC and HDFC Bank subsidiary providing retail, commercial vehicle, and enterprise loans across a ₹1.31 lakh crore asset base, with strong parentage constituting its primary competitive moat and funding advantage. Revenue growth has decelerated from a peak of +21.4% (Q3FY26) to +10.3% in H1 FY27 with loan growth similarly slowing from 14.1% to ~11%, while PAT recovered sharply to +36.2% YoY (₹1,565 cr in H1 FY27 vs -2% in H1 FY26) as GNPA improved from 2.81% to 2.43% and Net NPA from 1.34% to 1.09% — partially offset by structurally elevated credit costs (2.58% in FY26) and deeply negative cash conversion (CFO/PAT -0.34×), which flag earnings quality concerns. Using the P/B+ROE lender yardstick mandated by the sector card, P/B 2.79× against ROE 13.9% places the stock in fair territory (not cheap: P/B > 1.5×; not expensive: P/B < 3× with ROE > 12%); peer-relative ranking at P27 in the broad market and a ~40% discount to sector median P/B, combined with forward P/E 14.7× vs trailing 22.5×, suggest the market has already priced in a meaningful earnings recovery. The primary risk is that loan/AUM growth deceleration (tracking toward low-double-digits) persists in a RISK_OFF macro environment with rising crude costs and an elevated credit cost base, stalling the earnings normalisation that currently drives the bull case.

fundamental.thesis: HUDCO is a government-owned NBFC (NBFC-Upper Layer) that lends mainly to state agencies for housing and urban infrastructure. Its loan book is ₹1.87 lakh crore, up about 29% YoY. In H1 FY27, total income rose 25.7% YoY to ₹7,789 cr and PAT rose 31.5% to ₹1,762 cr, so the PAT margin widened to 22.6% from 21.6% a year ago. Growth has eased only slightly from the +28-29% pace of FY26, and asset quality is very clean: net credit-impaired assets are 0.04% with provision coverage of 93.8%. We grade valuation on price-to-book versus return on equity, the right measure for a lender, not P/E. P/B is about 2.35x against an ROE of roughly 16-20%, which is fair for a government lender; the low trailing P/E of 10.5x (forward 8.5x) adds some comfort but does not make it outright cheap. The main risk is concentration: borrowing is 7.2x equity and the book depends heavily on state-government infrastructure borrowers, so a slowdown in state spending or slow government repayments (such as the ₹743 cr Andrews Ganj claim on the housing ministry) would quickly squeeze growth and margins.

The underlying business is growing well: net interest income +29% to ₹4,228 cr, NIM up 40 bps YoY to 4.11%, advances +18%, deposits +17%, gross NPA down 53 bps to 2.12%, net NPA 0.17%, provision coverage 99.24% and capital adequacy 27.1%. fundamental.thesis: Indian Energy Exchange runs India's dominant power exchange, an asset-light trading platform where most revenue (77-78%) comes from transaction fees. Real-Time Market volumes have grown from 20% of its electricity volumes in FY23 to 41% in H1 FY27. In Q2FY27 revenue rose +10.8% YoY to ₹203 cr and PAT rose +12.9% to ₹139 cr, a 68.5% PAT margin. Revenue growth has slowed from +19.3% in Q1FY26 and +14.6% for FY26 to roughly 10-11% over the last three periods, though margins are steady to rising. Cash conversion is only moderate, with CFO/PAT of 0.73x in H1FY27 versus 0.88x in FY26. Because this is a fee-based exchange rather than a lender, I graded it on P/E and EV/EBITDA, not the bank P/B yardstick. On that basis it looks cheap: trailing P/E of 22.3x is 37% below the broad-market median of 35.2x, EV/EBITDA of 14.2x is at P24, ROE is 39%, and the stock sits at about 9% of its 52-week range. Part of that discount is fair given the regulatory overhang, and next-year earnings estimates have been cut 5.5% over 90 days, so the stock is not mispriced beyond doubt.

IFCI is a government-owned development finance institution. Most of its legacy lending book is still impaired, and much of its reported income comes from subsidiaries (such as its stock-broking and infrastructure arms) and treasury and recovery gains rather than from a healthy, growing loan book. The extracted filings show FY26 revenue of about ₹2,069 cr (+2.5% YoY) and PAT of ₹181 cr (+5.7%). Growth has slowed from +13.4% in H1FY26 to roughly flat, and PAT margin has narrowed from 13.6% in H1FY26 to 8.7% for the full year. The H1 FY27 results filed on 2026-11-12 show only credit-quality figures, with no revenue or PAT extracted yet, and the yfinance Q2FY27 row (₹604 cr revenue, ₹149 cr PAT) is unverified for a financial company. Credit quality is extremely weak and getting worse: gross NPA is 99.23% and net NPA 95.55% in H1 FY27, up from 95.79% and 78.44% in FY26, and the capital adequacy ratio (CRAR) is negative at -18.42%. For a lender, the right test is price-to-book against return on equity, and the stock fails it. P/B is 2.43x for a business earning about 0.7% ROA (FY26) with negative regulatory capital, so 'expensive' is the right grade, and the 119x trailing P/E (P96 against the broad market) confirms it. A P/B of 2.4x looks cheap only next to the broad-market median. The 23x forward P/E assumes a large earnings jump that the filings do not yet support. The biggest risk is that the price depends on government recapitalisation or restructuring hopes rather than on the core business. A disappointing H1 FY27 print, or any delay in capital support, could cut the valuation sharply. This is a midcap with thin disclosure, so conviction stays moderate.

The biggest fundamental risk is governance: the re-designation of co-founder R Venkataraman from Joint MD to Non-Executive Director on October 15 is a leadership change at a sensitive recovery juncture, compounded by a declining Provision Coverage Ratio (114% in Q3FY25 to 63% in H1FY26) and deeply negative cash conversion (CFO/PAT −7.34×), all of which limit conviction despite the appealing valuation.

fundamental.thesis: Jio Financial Services is a Reliance-group holding company whose value sits mainly in its Reliance Industries stake, with a fast-growing lending arm (Jio Credit), an asset-management joint venture (JioBlackRock), payments and insurance businesses. Manappuram Finance is India's second-largest listed gold-loan NBFC, with 5,375 branches and 46.9 lakh customers. It also owns a microfinance subsidiary, Asirvad, with ₹7,919 cr of loans. Part of the jump is a base effect: Q2FY26 profit was hit by heavy microfinance credit costs, and Asirvad is now back in profit at ₹32 cr. Because this is a lender, I graded valuation on price-to-book against return on equity, as the sector card says, not on P/E. P/B of 1.7x is fair to slightly cheap against a 15.2% annualised H1FY27 ROE. The 7% trailing ROE still includes last year's microfinance losses, and the forward P/E of 11.0x against a trailing 27.4x already prices in the recovery. With the stock at 86% of its 52-week range, I call it fair rather than cheap. The biggest risks are that loan growth depends heavily on gold prices, which are now falling, and that the Q2 release left out asset-quality figures (bad-loan ratio, provision cover) at a time when capital adequacy has dropped from 28.3% to 21.3% because of the fast loan growth.
