fundamental.thesis: Nuvama is a wealth management and capital markets firm (private wealth, broking, asset services and asset management). It is a fee and market-linked business, not a lender, so this is a cyclical, market-beta franchise. In the latest extracted quarter (Q1FY27) consolidated PAT rose 38.0% YoY to ₹305.64 cr from ₹221.48 cr at a steady 22.1% margin. That growth is low quality: capital markets revenue fell 15.6% YoY to ₹172.09 cr, ₹250.17 cr came from holding-company investment income, revenue growth fell from +107% in FY25 to -12.5% in FY26, and the Q2FY27 results filed on 2026-11-06 are not yet in the extracted data. On valuation I used P/B against ROE plus P/E, since AUM-linked earnings data is unavailable: P/B of 7.6x is backed by a 27.3% ROE, and the trailing P/E of 30.6x (forward 21.6x) sits near the broad-market median at P43. That makes it fair, not cheap, especially with the stock at 91% of its 52-week range and FY EPS estimates cut 1.9% over 30 days. The biggest risk is that earnings lean on investment income and market activity while the core capital markets line shrinks, and a fresh promoter encumbrance disclosure (2026-11-04) adds a governance flag for a midcap.

fundamental.thesis: One 97 Communications (Paytm) is a pre-scale digital payments and financial-services platform with net cash of Rs 12,714 cr, so we judge it on EV/sales, growth delivery and unit economics rather than lender P/B or trailing P/E. Q2 FY27, derived as H1 less Q1, shows revenue of about Rs 2,648 cr, up 28.5% YoY, with growth improving from +24.2% in Q2 FY26 to +27.6% in Q1 FY27; EBITDA margin rose from 8.3% to about 16.9% over the year, but PAT was nearly flat sequentially at about Rs 225 cr versus Rs 220 cr, and the 209% H1 PAT growth is flattered by a very low Rs 21 cr base in Q2 FY26. Valuation is fair but not cheap at about 6x EV/TTM sales (our calculation from market cap, net cash and filed revenue), mid-range in the 52-week band; the 128x trailing P/E and 112.9x EV/EBITDA look stale against about 79x annualised H1 PAT, while the 34.9x forward P/E already assumes about Rs 2,000 cr of PAT, roughly 2.25x the current run-rate. The biggest risk is that earnings fail to reach that level, especially as H1 free cash flow was only Rs 42 cr after Rs 434 cr of capex and cash fell Rs 790 cr, with FEMA and GST matters still unresolved.

fundamental.thesis: Piramal Finance is a diversified, mid-sized NBFC focused on retail lending (housing, secured and unsecured loans) while it runs down a legacy wholesale and DHFL-era book; AUM grew about 23% YoY as of Q3 FY26. Growth is strong and steady rather than accelerating: H1 FY27 revenue rose 27.3% YoY to ₹7,015 cr and PAT rose 66.8% to ₹1,006 cr, with implied Q2 revenue of about ₹3,585 cr (~+27% YoY) and PAT of ₹545 cr (+67%). Quarterly PAT margin widened from 13.4% in Q1 to about 15.2% in Q2, and gross NPA eased from 2.6% (Q3 FY26) to 2.26% (FY26); the pipeline's 'accelerating' label leans on an inconsistent 9M FY26 row, so I read revenue growth as stable at about 27%. On the P/B-plus-ROE yardstick the card prescribes for lenders, a P/B of 1.6x is modest, but trailing ROE is only 5.4% (FY26 ROA 1.41%), so it is not cheap on current returns. The trailing P/E of 30.2x sits above the 18–28x NBFC band, while the forward P/E of 13.8x prices in a sharp earnings ramp, which nets out to fair value, with the stock already at 89% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is that the ROE ramp the forward multiple assumes slips, through legacy-book drag, credit costs or the pending NCLT amalgamation, at a time when sell-side EPS estimates have been trimmed 2–3% over 30–90 days despite an 8/10 buy rating mix.

fundamental.thesis: PB Fintech runs Policybazaar and Paisabazaar, India's largest online marketplaces for insurance and credit. It earns commissions and does not lend, so the lender yardsticks in the Financials sector card (P/B plus ROE) do not fit, and the debt/equity figure of 4.92 is probably a data artefact, not real leverage. The latest quarter we can verify, Q1FY27, had revenue of ₹1,888 cr, up 40.0% year on year, faster than +37.0% in Q3FY26 and +36.5% for FY26 as a whole. PAT was ₹163 cr, up 92%, but PAT margin has slipped from 10.7% to 9.9% to 8.6% and EBITDA margin from 11.2% to 7.4%, so growth is costing more margin than before. Q2FY27 numbers have not been extracted from the filed results; the yfinance figure of ₹773 cr revenue does not match a ₹1,888 cr Q1 run-rate, so it was ignored. Judged as a high-growth platform on price-to-sales and growth, the stock looks expensive: P/S is 11.0x, EV/EBITDA is 140.6x (99th percentile of the broad market), trailing P/E is 111x and forward P/E is 47.8x (91st percentile). That is a full price even for ~40% growth, while next-year earnings estimates have been cut 15.1% over 90 days and 7.9% over 30 days. The biggest risk is that the premium multiple shrinks if margins keep falling while analysts keep cutting estimates.

fundamental.thesis: SBFC Finance is a mid-sized, profitable NBFC lender classed by RBI as Middle Layer, with gross loans of Rs 11,161 cr and ROA of about 4.6%. Q2 FY27 revenue rose 33.0% YoY to Rs 547 cr, up from an implied +26.5% in Q1 (the pre-computed 'decelerating' signal mixes quarterly, half-year and full-year periods), but PAT growth slowed to +27.2% at Rs 139 cr from +34.0% in Q3 FY26, PAT margin slipped from 27.7% to 25.4% over the same three quarters, and AUM growth eased from 30.7% at FY26 to 27.0%. Using P/B against ROE, the right yardstick for a lender, valuation is fair at 2.71x book for a 13.0% ROE (about 2.5x on reported net worth of Rs 4,049 cr), with the 22.43x trailing P/E inside the 18-28x NBFC range only as a cross-check, while the P29 peer rank carries little weight because it compares against the broad market and the stated +38.8% target upside looks overstated because the 52-week position implies a price near Rs 92, or about +26%. The biggest risk is that fast loan growth is outrunning the safety cushion: gross NPA improved from 2.77% to 2.6%, but net NPA is stuck near 1.5%, provision coverage fell from 46.2% to 42.2%, and debt-to-equity rose from 1.80 to 2.31.

fundamental.thesis: RBL Bank is a mid-size private sector lender undergoing a transformative reset — the recently RBI-approved amalgamation of Emirates NBD's Indian branches has materially scaled the balance sheet (advances +42% YoY to ₹1,42,314 cr) while an in-progress asset-quality clean-up has reduced GNPA from 2.78% six quarters ago to 1.02% today, the strongest trajectory signal in this pack. Q2FY27 delivered a step-change: net total income grew +29% YoY to ₹3,208 cr (NII component +37% at ₹2,131 cr, NIM expanding to 4.61%) and PAT surged +170% YoY to ₹482 cr (PAT margin: 15.0%), accelerating sharply from the +2.5%/+27% prints in Q1FY27 and reversing the -20% PAT decline seen in Q2FY26 — direction is unambiguously improving. Using P/B + ROE, the appropriate yardstick for lenders per the Sector Card: at P/B 1.36× the stock is optically below the cheap threshold, but ROE of 4.43% is mechanically depressed by an outsized CAR of 30.1% (2× typical regulatory minimums), making fair the more honest grade — the market has partially re-rated the name (stock at 96.2% of 52-week range) and at P33 on trailing P/E the consensus-peer view corroborates a fair assessment rather than a screaming-cheap one. The biggest risk is the sustained CASA ratio decline from 32.5% (Q1FY26) to 27.2% (Q2FY27), signalling a weakening liability franchise and rising cost of funds that could cap NIM improvement as the excess capital gets progressively deployed into the loan book.

fundamental.thesis: Star Health is a health-focused insurer, with ₹9,635 cr of H1 FY27 revenue from its health segment (up 13%) out of ₹10,856 cr in total. H1 FY27 revenue rose 10.4% to ₹10,856 cr and PAT rose 57.3% to ₹815 cr, but the 'accelerating' and 'expanding' trend signals are unreliable because they mix H1, Q1, 9M and full-year periods across an Ind AS restatement; underlying profitability looks weaker, with PAT falling from ₹550 cr in Q1 to an implied ₹265 cr in Q2, the combined operating ratio worsening from 92.33% to 94.52%, and the claims ratio at 68.95%. Using P/B against ROE as the closest available yardstick (the sector card names none for general insurers and the peer set is only a broad-market fallback), valuation is expensive at 3.32x book for a 7.5% ROE, although a forward P/E of 20.4x versus a trailing 50.48x and FY EPS estimates up 6.7% in 30 days show the market expects a sharp earnings recovery; the price input also needs checking, because the consensus upside implies about ₹511 while market cap and the 52-week position imply about ₹572. The biggest risk is that this recovery fails to arrive if underwriting keeps weakening, and earnings quality is already a concern with operating cash flow down 54% to ₹611 cr, CFO/PAT at 0.75x, and the reported ₹40,000 cr NCD redemption looking like an extraction error since it exceeds the ₹33,654 cr market cap.

fundamental.thesis: Tata Capital is a large diversified NBFC, with AUM of Rs 3.08L cr (+26% YoY) that is 85.4% retail and SME. In Q2 FY27, net total income rose 24% to Rs 4,676 cr and PAT rose 51% to Rs 1,660 cr, with credit cost easing to 0.9% from 1.3%, ROA improving to 2.3% from 1.9%, and gross Stage 3 at 1.9%; PAT growth stayed strong at +56% in Q1 and +51% in Q2, but the table's 'decelerating revenue' and 'contracting margin' signals are unreliable because it mixes gross revenue with net income, and H1 PAT of Rs 3,460 cr also exceeds the Q1 and Q2 sum of Rs 3,288 cr. Using P/B against ROE, the lender yardstick named in the sector card rather than the 29.35x trailing P/E, the stock looks fair but full at 3.83x reported book (about 3.1x using Rs 47,778 cr equity and the Rs 1.5L cr market cap) for 12-14% ROE, at 69% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is that recent profit growth leans partly on lower credit costs while capital adequacy has fallen from 20.3% to 19% to 17.3%, with next-year EPS estimates cut 1.6% and no guidance captured in the recent extracted periods.

fundamental.thesis: Union Bank of India is a large public-sector lender, and its asset quality and loan growth are clearly getting better. In Q2 FY27, total income rose only +3.2% YoY to ₹32,809 cr, but PAT jumped +29.9% to ₹5,537 cr, pushing the PAT margin up to 16.9% from 13.4% a year ago. Under the hood the trend is clean: NIM rose from 2.67% to 2.86% over four quarters, gross NPA fell from 3.29% to 2.42%, net NPA fell to 0.42%, credit cost is low at 0.21%, and loan growth sped up from about 5% to about 13% YoY. Using the P/B-plus-ROE yardstick for lenders (P/E is ignored for banks), the stock trades at 1.01× book against a 15.7% TTM ROE (17.2% in Q2), so it is cheap. fundamental.thesis: Kaynes Technology India is an integrated EMS (Electronics Manufacturing Services) company — one of India's leading players in PCB assembly, OSAT, and box-build for industrial, automotive, and aerospace verticals — positioned as a direct beneficiary of the China+1 manufacturing shift and PLI electronics incentives. Q1FY27 revenue grew +40.4% YoY to ₹946 cr (aided by subsidiary consolidation), but this top-line strength masked severe profitability deterioration: PAT fell 24.4% YoY to ₹56 cr with PAT margin compressing to 5.9% from 11.1% in Q1FY26 — a 480 bps contraction — driven by finance costs surging 30.7% YoY from QIP-funded capex and a higher effective tax rate (35.8% vs 27.9%), with FCF deeply negative at -₹106 cr (CFO/PAT -1.79×). Using EV/EBITDA of 39× as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive Industrials name (per sector card), the stock sits at the 80th percentile of broad-market peers on both forward P/E and EV/EBITDA; the 52-week position at 10.8% of range reflects market-led de-rating, not a mispriced entry — expensive given negative FCF and contracting margins. The thesis hinges entirely on whether ₹10,600 cr in cumulative OSAT and PCB capex (funded across two large QIPs totalling ₹30,000 cr and a D/E of 19.17) converts to operating leverage within 2–3 quarters, which 90-day EPS cuts of 10.5% and a 9-of-23 sell rating from the sell side suggest is far from assured.

Jupiter Wagons is a mid-cap maker of rail freight wagons and related products (wheelsets, Stone India brake systems, battery energy storage systems via JEM), so its revenue comes from working through its order book. The last results we have extracted are FY26, filed May 2026: revenue fell 26.0% YoY to ₹2,961 cr and PAT fell 56.0% to ₹166 cr. PAT margin dropped from 9.6% to 5.7% and EBITDA margin from 14.6% to 12.4%, and the order book shrank from ₹5,538 cr (H1FY26) to ₹4,675 cr, only about 1.6x revenue against the roughly 3x the sector treats as solid visibility. The Q1FY27 numbers are missing and the Q2FY27 results filed on 13-Nov have not been extracted yet, so management's claimed Q2 recovery in production is unconfirmed. Using EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for an order-book business, the stock trades at 30.0x (P66 vs broad-market peers). Trailing P/E is 69.7x, well above the 28–45x Industrials range, and P/B is 4.0x on an ROE of just 5.8%. That makes it expensive, unless the 28.4x forward P/E is backed by a sharp earnings rebound. Sell-side views point the other way: FY-EPS estimates have been cut 15.1% over 90 days and next-FY estimates 6.6% over 30 days, which is a classic pattern before a stock de-rates. Some snapshot fields look unreliable: the 69% dividend yield, the debt/equity reading of 33.37 (probably 0.33x quoted as a percentage) and a consensus target that doesn't match the 52-week range.

FY26 revenues grew +21.7% YoY to ₹7,701 cr (accelerating from just +4.0% in Q3FY25), with B2B driving 25.5% volume growth and PAT advancing +17.4% to ₹574 cr; critically, FY26 CFO/PAT of 1.62× confirms earnings quality, though EBITDA margin compressed 118 bps and the unverified yfinance Q1FY27 print (~+16% revenue YoY, PAT down ~17% YoY) signals a tentative growth deceleration requiring PDF confirmation. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for a capital-intensive industrial, PTCIL trades at 203× EV/EBITDA (sector median 28–45×) and 259× trailing P/E, ranking at P100 (most expensive) among 473 market peers, while a P/B of 18.4× against a 7% ROE and Debt/Equity of 17.34× signals extreme valuation risk with no earnings support. Sustained EPS estimate cuts (-13.1% over 90 days, -14.6% on next-FY) while sell-side ratings stay uniformly bullish is a textbook pre-derating pattern, and any further slip in the defence order pipeline or margin recovery could catalyse a 30–50% de-rating — the historical norm for industrial cycle disappointments.

RHI Magnesita India is the country's largest refractories maker, majority-owned by the Austrian RHI Magnesita group. Its fortunes depend mainly on steel and cement capacity use, so it behaves more like a Materials supplier than an order-book Industrials name. Revenue growth has slowed in every period, from +14.3% in H1FY26 to +5.6% in Q1FY27 and +2.4% in H1FY27. Q2FY27, worked out as H1 minus Q1, was about ₹1,030 cr, roughly -0.6% YoY. PAT tells a better story: Q2 PAT was about ₹62 cr against ₹38 cr a year ago (+63%), and the PAT margin rose from 3.7% to about 6.0%. These figures are compared against a weak base, and the margin fell back from Q1, when EBITDA margin was 14.5%, to about 11.1% in Q2. Trailing P/E is not meaningful because of the large FY26 goodwill impairment, so I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA. At 17.8x (P34, 24% below the broad-market median), with forward P/E at 20.2x and P/B at 2.1x, the stock looks fair for a capital-intensive maker whose sales have stalled. The 52-week position of 22% gives a decent entry, but next-year EPS estimates were cut 3.4% over 90 days. The main risk is that flat volumes from steel customers turn into falling margins, at the same time as the CFO is leaving at year-end.

The biggest risk is that tanker rates fall back as Middle East disruption eases. On top of that come stress in the LNG joint ventures (₹240 cr ILT-3 provision; auditors flag going-concern doubts at ILT-1/2/3), board committees still short of SEBI listing-rule requirements, and a government stake sale stuck since 2020.

RITES is a government-owned (PSU) railway and infrastructure consultancy, turnkey-projects and rolling-stock export company with an order book of ₹9,388 cr, about 4.0x its trailing revenue, which gives it more than two years of revenue visibility. Q2FY27 revenue was ₹583 cr, up only 0.7% YoY, so growth has slowed from +10.0% in FY26 and +5.7% in Q3FY26. PAT fell 8.0% YoY at a 19.5% margin, and EBITDA fell 10.5%, because export revenue almost disappeared (down 99.2%) and consultancy revenue dropped 4.3%. Turnkey revenue grew 65.9%, but that did not offset the other two. Following the sector card, I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA plus order-book quality: EV/EBITDA is 16.9x against a peer median of 23.3x (P31), and trailing P/E is 24.85x, below the 28–45x Industrials band. That discount looks deserved rather than a mispricing, because Q2 order inflow was only ₹446 cr against ₹583 cr of revenue (book-to-bill below 1), FY EPS estimates were cut 6% over 90 days, and H1FY26 cash conversion was weak at 0.22x CFO/PAT, so I grade it fair. The main risk is that the recovery in H2 depends on the Bangladesh coach exports starting on time. Note also that the 361% dividend yield in the data feed is clearly a data error, so I ignored it; the 97% payout ratio is the reliable dividend figure.

fundamental.thesis: Schneider Electric Infrastructure is a midcap maker of medium-voltage switchgear and electrical distribution equipment. It is positioned in India's power-transmission, data-centre, semiconductor-fab and renewables build-out, with record Q2 FY27 orders of ₹1,265 cr (+50.9% YoY) and an order backlog of ₹2,701 cr (+49.6% YoY). EBITDA margin fell from 13.6% to 8.4%, and H1 PAT was down 55%, because the company could not pass on copper, aluminium and steel costs fast enough and finance costs rose about 39%. We grade valuation on EV/EBITDA, the yardstick for capital-intensive industrials. At 76.6× (P96 vs the broad market, versus a median of 23.3×), a 146.8× trailing P/E, 55.3× forward P/E and a price at 86% of its 52-week range, the stock is clearly expensive. That price assumes the H2 margin recovery management promises, which is not yet visible. The biggest risk is that margins stay weak while analysts keep cutting earnings estimates (FY EPS -30% over 30 days, -44% over 90 days). That pattern of cuts against a still-bullish rating mix often comes before a de-rating in richly valued industrials.

fundamental.thesis: Techno Electric is a mid-cap power transmission and distribution EPC contractor with a growing data-centre business. Using EV/EBITDA as the yardstick for a capital-intensive order-book business, it trades at 19.4x, about 17% below the market median (P40); trailing P/E of 26.2x is just under the 28–45x Industrials band. The stock is near its 52-week low, which helps entry risk, so I grade valuation fair rather than cheap because cash conversion is weak (CFO/PAT 0.19x in H1, negative in FY26) and FY EPS estimates were cut 14.9% in the last 30 days. The biggest risk is that profit is not turning into cash: about ₹590 cr of Afghanistan receivables depend on an uncertain ADB/UNOPS payment process, and a ₹212 cr Bengal Energy arbitration has been open since 2012.

fundamental.thesis: Tega Industries makes wear-resistant consumables and grinding equipment for global mining and mineral processing. In June 2026 it bought Molycop, a much larger grinding-media business, and this has made the latest numbers hard to compare with last year. Consolidated H1FY27 revenue was ₹5,978 cr, against ₹1,692 cr for all of FY26, and the company reported a PAT loss of ₹167 cr (-2.8% margin). That loss is mainly a non-cash acquisition accounting charge, but Molycop also lost ₹150 cr on an adjusted basis in its first 4 months. The pre-acquisition business is mixed: consumables revenue grew about 30% YoY with EBITDA margin up to 22.4%, and the ex-Molycop order book grew 21%, but the equipment segment shrank and management cut FY27 equipment growth guidance from 25% to 15%. Consolidated EBITDA margin has fallen from 20-21% to 14.0% over the trend window. On EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-intensive order-book business, the stock looks expensive. EV/EBITDA is 51.7x (P90 vs the broad market, +122% vs the 23.3x median) and trailing P/E is 88.8x, well above the 28-45x Industrials range. ROE is only 5.9%, and sell-side FY EPS estimates have been cut 51-56% over 30-90 days. The biggest risk is the debt taken on to fund the deal: borrowings rose from about ₹318 cr to about ₹11,492 cr while Molycop is still loss-making. Integration, and how much cash the combined business can generate, now decide the equity story more than the base business does.

fundamental.thesis: Tata Motors (TMCV) is India's largest commercial vehicle maker, with 36.2% domestic share in H1 FY27 and 55.7% in heavy trucks, and it holds net cash of Rs 15,900 cr before the Iveco deal. Revenue growth accelerated from +16.1% in Q3 FY26 to +19.3% in Q1 FY27 and +36.3% in Q2 FY27 (Rs 25,338 cr on 42% wholesale volume growth), but EBITDA margin slipped from 11.3% to 10.9% YoY and PAT fell from Rs 2,556 cr in Q1 to Rs 1,253 cr in Q2 (5.0% margin) after a Rs 708 cr fair-value loss; management guides to tapering growth and a 150-200 bps commodity headwind in Q3, so the pre-computed 'expanding' PAT margin signal and the 17.1% Q1 EBITDA margin (it conflicts with 10.9% for both H1 and Q2) should not be relied on. Valuation is fair using EV/EBITDA, the yardstick for this capital-intensive business: 16.8x is 28% below the broad-market median of 23.3x (P30), and forward P/E of 18.5x sits at the low end of the 18-28x auto range with estimates up 10.1% over 90 days, but the trailing P/E of 49.5x (distorted by fair-value losses) and P/B of 11.8x (P87) limit the cheapness case, and the peer set is a broad-market fallback rather than true CV peers. The biggest risk is the Iveco acquisition, whose final tender outcome, funding and integration burden are not visible in the data provided and could erode the net cash position just as the CV cycle's growth rates are guided to slow, while the auditor resignation filed on 2026-10-31 remains unexplained here.

Titagarh Rail Systems is a mid-cap maker of railway wagons and passenger coaches (including metro and Vande Bharat-type programmes), and it benefits from the government rail-capex cycle. Revenue growth has slowed sharply: Q2FY27 revenue, derived as H1 FY27 ₹1,558 cr minus Q1 ₹765 cr, comes to about ₹793 cr, roughly +0.6% YoY against ₹788 cr, after +12.6% in Q1. PAT of about ₹63 cr (7.9% margin, versus 6.0% a year ago) and the 13.8% EBITDA margin show better profitability, but the +375% H1 PAT jump mostly reflects a restated prior-year base hit by the Italian associate Firema's losses, not underlying demand. On EV/EBITDA, which is the right yardstick for an order-book Industrials business, the stock trades at 35.8x (P75 vs the broad market) with a trailing P/E of 103x, ROE of 4.9% and the price at 90.5% of its 52-week range, so it is expensive. The 26x forward P/E depends on a profit rebound that analysts are cutting fast, with FY-EPS estimates down 13.5% in 30 days and 21.3% in 90 days even though all 9 ratings are Buy. Free cash flow is negative (-₹77 cr in H1, with ₹230 cr of capex), and no order-book or order-inflow data was provided to check revenue visibility.

On valuation, using EV/EBITDA as the card's yardstick for capital-goods names, the stock trades at 45.5x EV/EBITDA (86th percentile, about 95% above the market median) and 61x trailing P/E, above the 28–45x Industrials range. fundamental.thesis: Waaree Energies is India's largest solar module maker. It is integrating backward into cells, inverters, BESS and polysilicon, and it now runs India's largest retail solar distribution network, with 700+ franchises. In Q2 FY27 revenue grew +23.9% YoY to ₹7,518 cr, but growth has slowed sharply from +118.8% in Q3 FY26 to +79.2% in Q1 FY27 and +23.9% now. PAT fell -14.2% YoY to ₹754 cr as operating EBITDA margin dropped 540 bps to 17.8%. The positives are that management held its FY27 operating EBITDA guidance of ₹7,000–7,700 cr, cash conversion is strong (H1 CFO/PAT 2.1x, net cash ₹3,224 cr) and the order book of ₹59,200 cr covers 2.2x revenue. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the yardstick for capital-intensive Industrials. At 11.3x it is about 50% below the broad-market median (P15). Trailing P/E is 19.8x (P22) and forward P/E is 15.9x, both far below Industrials norms, so the stock is optically cheap. The discount is partly earned: margins are shrinking, sell-side EPS estimates were cut about 6-7% over 90 days, and new order inflow fell to ₹7,300 cr from ₹20,500 cr. The biggest risk is a global module glut (utilisation fell to 45% from 71%) combined with US Section 232 and AD/CVD duties, which cut the overseas mix from 47% to 18.5%. Together these could keep pushing margins and the multiple lower.

H1 FY27 revenue rose 14.8% YoY to ₹2,021 cr and PAT rose 28.2% to ₹271 cr, a big step up from the +1–6% growth seen through FY26. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA because this is a capital-intensive business. At 19.4x EV/EBITDA and 28.3x trailing P/E (21.2x forward), it trades about 17–19% below the broad-market median (P38–P49 on peer rank) but sits at the top of the Materials P/E range, so overall it is fair. With the stock at 77% of its 52-week range and no management guidance, the upside looks limited. The main risks are the pending ED/CBI proceedings over ₹190 cr of attached land in Ranchi (hearings on Nov 28 and Dec 4) and weaker cash conversion: H1 CFO/PAT fell to 0.78x from 1.42x in FY26 as working capital built up. Note that the live debt/equity of 6.92 and dividend yield of 75% look like data errors (probably percent-scale), so I did not use them.

Deepak Fertilisers is an integrated maker of industrial chemicals and fertilisers. It leads several Indian niches, with roughly 60% market share in concentrated nitric acid, 40% in technical ammonium nitrate (TAN) and 38% in isopropyl alcohol (IPA) in West India. In Q2FY27 revenue was ₹3,334 cr, up 10.9% YoY. That is a small slowdown from about +12% in FY26. PAT jumped 83.9% YoY to ₹394 cr, and PAT margin widened to 11.8% from 6.4% in FY26, with EBITDA margin up 706 bps to 22.5%. The gains came from chemicals, where revenue rose 42.5% on the Equinor gas contract and tight IPA supply, while crop nutrition revenue fell 12.8% on a weak monsoon. This is a chemicals and fertiliser cyclical, so I graded valuation mainly on EV/EBITDA, as the sector card says. At 11.1x it is above the card's 5–8x mid-cycle norm for chemicals. Trailing P/E of 16.9x sits inside the 12–22x Materials range, and forward P/E of 10.6x prices in continued growth. Taken together that is fair, not cheap. The 'bottom quartile' peer rank compares it against the whole market rather than true industry peers, so I gave it little weight. The biggest risk is that the margin jump depends on cyclical supports: tight IPA supply and the gas contract benefit. Meanwhile the Dahej nitric acid and Gopalpur TAN plants, both 98% complete with start-up targeted for Q4 FY27, still have to ramp up into a market where nitric acid prices are under pressure.

fundamental.thesis: Jain Resource Recycling is a non-ferrous metal recycler that makes copper, lead and aluminium from scrap. It is a commodity-spread business, recently listed, and copper is now about two-thirds of its revenue. Revenue is growing fast, but much of that comes from copper prices and profit is not keeping up. H1 FY27 revenue rose 65.5% YoY to ₹6,061 cr while PAT rose only 3.1% to ₹160 cr. Taking Q1 out of H1 suggests Q2 FY27 revenue of about ₹3,337 cr (around +58% YoY, slower than Q1's +75.9%) and PAT of about ₹91 cr, which is roughly 8% lower than a year ago. EBITDA margin has fallen from 7.0% (9M FY26) to 5.7% (Q1) to 4.5% (H1), and PAT margin from 4.4% to about 2.7%. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA because the sector card says to judge cyclical, commodity-spread businesses that way. On that measure the stock looks expensive. EV/EBITDA is 25.1×, against roughly 5–8× for cyclicals at mid-cycle, and trailing P/E is 35.8×, against a 12–22× Materials benchmark. The 19.9× forward P/E depends on earnings growth, but analysts have cut those estimates by about 19% over the last 90 days. The biggest risk is that margins keep shrinking while net debt is high (about 3.3× EBITDA, debt/equity about 82%). If copper prices or recycling spreads reverse, earnings could fall sharply.

fundamental.thesis: J.K. Cement is a mid-sized cement maker that is also building a paints business through its subsidiary JK Maxx Paints. A new ₹130 cr, 75,000 KLPA plant in Telangana is funded from a ₹600 cr paints budget. In Q1FY27, revenue grew 20.3% YoY to ₹4,032 cr, but PAT fell 15.3% YoY to ₹275 cr. EBITDA margin has slid from 19.5% (H1FY26) to 17.0% and PAT margin from 7.5% to 6.8%, so volume growth is not reaching profits. The Q2FY27 results were filed on 2026-10-24 but have not been extracted yet, and the yfinance quarterly rows (₹513 cr revenue) are clearly inconsistent with the filings and were ignored. On valuation, I used EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive business: 18.8× is below the broad-market median of 23.3×, but trailing P/E of 40.8× is far above the 12–22× Materials benchmark. Forward P/E of 25.6× depends on an earnings recovery that analysts are actively cutting (FY EPS estimates down 9.3% over 90 days), so I grade it expensive, even though cement usually commands a premium and the stock sits at 13.7% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is further margin compression in a crude-up, weak-rupee, risk-off environment, made worse by spending on paints, a segment the sector card describes as structurally broken by Birla Opus's entry.

Hindustan Copper is India's only vertically integrated copper miner, a state-owned company whose earnings move with global copper prices; it judges best as a commodity cyclical, not a consumer franchise. Q2 FY27, worked out as H1 minus Q1, delivered revenue of about ₹1,176 cr (+64% YoY) and PAT of about ₹518 cr (+181% YoY). H1 FY27 revenue rose 71% to ₹2,112 cr and PAT rose 174% to ₹870 cr. EBITDA margin widened from about 42% to 58% over the trend window, and H1 cash conversion was sound: CFO/PAT 0.97x, free cash flow ₹601 cr. On EV/EBITDA, the yardstick the sector card sets for commodity names, the stock trades at 33.4x against a typical 5-8x mid-cycle range for cyclicals, and its trailing P/E of 53.5x is far above the 12-22x Materials benchmark. Even the forward P/E of 25.6x is still above that range, so the stock is expensive and already prices in copper staying high. The biggest risk is that the margin expansion comes mostly from copper prices rather than volume, so a fall in copper prices could cut earnings sharply while the multiples are high. Two smaller flags: the reported debt/equity of 3.32 does not match finance costs of only ₹5.45 cr, so that figure looks unreliable, and there was a recent exchange fine for corporate-governance non-compliance.

fundamental.thesis: Linde India is a subsidiary of the global Linde group that makes industrial gases and also runs a lower-margin project engineering arm. Gases bring in about 71% of segment revenue at a 26.4% segment margin, while project engineering earns only 9.8%. The latest extracted quarter, Q1FY27, shows revenue of ₹694 cr, up 21.6% YoY, but PAT fell 2.4% YoY to ₹105 cr. PAT margin has slipped to 15.1% from the low-to-mid 20s in earlier periods, and the H1 EBITDA margin dropped 850 bps to 31.8%. In short, sales are growing faster but that growth is not reaching profit, and heavy capex (about 96% of H1 revenue) pushed free cash flow to -₹647 cr. Industrial gases is a utility-like business, not a steel or cement cyclical, so I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA and peer multiples. fundamental.thesis: Nuvoco Vistas is an East- and North-focused cement and ready-mix concrete (RMC) maker with about 35 MTPA of target capacity. It is a mid-tier player in a sector where UltraTech and Adani now control about 45% of capacity. Using the filings trend table (the yfinance rows are inconsistent and were ignored), Q2FY27 revenue rose 13.5% YoY to ₹2,790 cr, up from +9.0% in Q1, and cement volumes grew 9% YoY against 5% in Q1. Profit quality is thinner than the headline suggests. PAT rose 78% YoY, but only to ₹65 cr, a 2.3% margin. EBITDA margin fell to 14.7% from 18.3% in Q1 and 15.1% a year ago. Implied EBITDA per tonne is about ₹875, below the healthy ₹900–1,100 band and down from roughly ₹1,080 in Q1. Valuation is graded on EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-intensive cement maker, not P/E. At 8.6x (P8 of the broad market, no close peers in the universe), with P/B of 1.09x, forward P/E of 20.5x against trailing 31x, and the price at 18% of its 52-week range, the stock looks cheap against typical cement multiples. Much of that discount is justified by an ROE of only 3.7% and high debt. The biggest risk is the balance sheet. Net debt is ₹5,028 cr, current ratio is 0.57x, free cash flow was -₹246 cr in H1 because of capex, and legal disputes are pending: the ₹490 cr CCI penalty and about ₹454 cr of West Bengal incentive provisions. These come on top of rising crude and a weak rupee pushing up fuel and freight costs.

NMDC Steel runs a single integrated 3 MTPA steel plant at Nagarnar. It was demerged from NMDC Ltd, the Government of India still holds 50.79%, and a strategic sale is pending; as a mid-sized, state-controlled mill it takes market prices for its steel. In Q1FY27, revenue grew 8.8% YoY to ₹3,662 cr and PAT was ₹51 cr (+97.6% YoY), a 1.4% PAT margin. EBITDA margin has improved from -37.9% (Q3FY25) to -20.2% (FY25), 7.9% (9MFY26) and 12.1% now, but revenue growth has slowed sharply from +129–179% to +8.8% as the plant's ramp-up base effect fades. For a steel mill I grade on EV/EBITDA, not P/E, because a 235.6x P/E on near-zero profit means little: at 11.7x it sits well above the 5–8x mid-cycle range for steel cyclicals, and P/B of 1.05x with ROE of 0.4% is not cheap either. So I rate it expensive on the right yardstick, even though it ranks P17 on EV/EBITDA against a broad-market peer set that isn't comparable. The biggest risk is debt: a debt service coverage ratio of 0.17 against an SBI term loan of about ₹3,177 cr (finance costs ₹126 cr a quarter) leaves almost no room if steel spreads narrow. Note that the Q2FY27 results (board-approved 2026-11-12) are not yet in the data, and the latest annual figures held are FY25, so FY26 is stale.

fundamental.thesis: NMDC is India's largest iron-ore miner. It is a state-owned company that has to accept global iron-ore prices, and it has a net cash pile of ₹8,188 cr, so its balance sheet is strong. Growth has nearly stopped. H1FY27 revenue rose only 2.4% YoY to ₹13,433 cr, and PAT fell 0.6% to ₹3,645 cr, down from +27% revenue and +15% PAT growth a year earlier. Q2FY27, worked out as H1 minus Q1, comes to about ₹6,638 cr revenue (+4% YoY) and ₹1,669 cr PAT (about −2%). H1 EBITDA fell 15% YoY to ₹4,712 cr because royalties and levies rose to 47% of revenue. Earnings also only partly turn into cash: operating cash flow was 0.75x of PAT. Because mining is capital-intensive and cyclical, I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA: 7.8x sits at the top of the 5–8x mid-cycle range for cyclicals. Trailing P/E of 10.4x is below the 12–22x Materials range, and P/B of 2.3x comes with a 23% ROE, so the stock is fair rather than clearly cheap given flat earnings. A few snapshot figures look wrong: the 397% dividend yield, the 18.8 debt/equity (which clashes with the net-cash position), and the analyst target upside, which doesn't match the 52-week position. The biggest risks sit off the income statement: a ₹16,189 cr contingent liability under Karnataka's mineral-rights tax and about ₹10,500 cr owed by struggling NMDC Steel and RINL.

Aster DM Healthcare is now one of India's largest hospital chains after its merger with Quality Care (CARE Hospitals) took effect on 1 July 2026, with 38 hospitals and 10,840 beds across 27 cities and a plan to reach about 15,070 beds by FY30. In Q2 FY27 revenue was ₹2,829 cr, up 19% YoY, and PAT was ₹281 cr, up 34% (about 9.9% margin). Occupancy rose 335 bps to 68% and patient volumes grew 12%. H1 FY27 revenue grew 20% and normalised PAT grew 27%. The pre-computed trend signals mix half-year and quarter rows and mislabel the direction, so only one clean quarter is usable and there is no proper multi-quarter trend. Using EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-intensive hospital business, the stock looks expensive. EV/EBITDA is 45.9x, about 97% above the broad-market median (P87), trailing P/E is 123x, P/B is 8.9x against a ROE of only 10.1%, and the price sits at 85% of its 52-week range. The forward P/E of 41x already assumes the merger synergies arrive. The biggest worry is that FY-EPS estimates have been cut about 18% in 30 days while all 12 analysts still rate it a buy, a pattern that often comes before a de-rating.

fundamental.thesis: Max Healthcare is one of India's largest listed hospital chains, with about 6,100 network beds running at more than 75% occupancy. NATCO Pharma is a mid-cap specialty generics maker whose profits have depended heavily on limited-competition US launches, mainly generic Revlimid (lenalidomide). In Q2 FY27, revenue fell 30.4% YoY to ₹1,019cr and PAT fell 60.9% to ₹203cr, as International Formulations dropped 41.4% to ₹668cr and PAT margin shrank from 42.6% in FY25 to 19.9%. Revenue did rise 28% from Q1, and the domestic business grew 38%, but neither is large enough to make up for the lost US windfall. Graded on P/E and EV/EBITDA, the stock looks cheap at first glance: trailing P/E is 11.2x against the 28–40x pharma band, EV/EBITDA is 9.6x and it ranks around P10 versus peers. But trailing earnings still include Revlimid profits that are not run-rate, and forward P/E is 19.3x, well above trailing, as earnings fall. Adjusted for that, I grade it fair rather than cheap. The biggest risk is that earnings keep falling after the lenalidomide patent cliff while cash generation weakens: H1 cash from operations was only ₹61cr against ₹276cr of capex, giving negative free cash flow and a cash-from-operations/PAT ratio of 0.30x.

fundamental.thesis: CEAT is India's #4 tyre maker (global rank #4 by brand) with 51% replacement, 30% OEM, and 19% export mix, operating at 95% capacity utilisation across ~80,000 daily tyres — a capital-intensive ancillary with defensive replacement demand. Q2FY27 revenue grew a strong +26.2% YoY to ₹4,762 cr, but PAT collapsed -39.8% YoY to ₹112 cr as EBITDA margins contracted sharply from ~13–14% (FY26/Q3FY26) to just 9.5% today — this is the defining trajectory: top-line accelerating while margins are structurally compressing, driven by commodity cost headwinds from the West Asia conflict and the Camso acquisition integration costs; the DSCR of 0.84× (below the 1.0× sustainability floor) and a current ratio of 0.67× flag tightening liquidity. Valuation looks outright cheap: EV/EBITDA at 7.4× sits at P5 vs the broad market (median 23.3×), trailing P/E of 20.2× is at P23 vs peers and -43% below market median — using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive business, the stock screens as cheap, but the multiple compression is warranted given the margin collapse, and forward P/E of 15.1× implies the market expects earnings recovery, which is far from assured. The single biggest risk is that commodity costs (natural rubber, crude derivatives) persist or worsen into H2FY27, keeping EBITDA margins pinned at 9–10% and preventing the earnings recovery the forward P/E demands — a second consecutive quarter of PAT decline would trigger a meaningful derating.

fundamental.thesis: Nava is a diversified midcap that earns money from a coal-fired power plant and coal mining in Zambia (MEL), merchant and captive thermal power in India, and ferro-alloy (silico-manganese) production in Odisha. It is a power-and-metals cyclical, not a regulated utility like NTPC or POWERGRID. In Q1FY27, consolidated revenue was ₹1,212 cr, up only 1.6% YoY. PAT was ₹333 cr, down 16.6% YoY from ₹399 cr, and EBITDA fell 7.0% YoY to ₹584 cr. Revenue growth has slowed from +20.9% in Q3FY26 to +7.7% for FY26 and +1.6% now. The big QoQ jump (PAT +144%) mostly recovers from a weak Q4, helped by higher plant load factors (India 85.4%, Zambia 89.3%), and does not mark a new uptrend. Cash conversion is a real positive: operating cash flow was 2.9x PAT in FY26, with ₹505 cr of free cash flow. I graded valuation mainly on EV/EBITDA because this is a capital-intensive business. At 10.0x EV/EBITDA, 1.79x P/B and 20.9x trailing P/E, the stock sits in the bottom quartile of the broad market (P10 on EV/EBITDA, P14 on P/B), but its P/E is above the 10–18x utilities band. Once you allow for Zambia country risk and cyclical earnings, I'd call it fair rather than clearly cheap. The near-term risks are the Q2FY27 results on 12 Nov 2026, the Odisha 60MW plant shutdown in September, and the 300MW MEL Phase 2 delay to mid-2028, which pushes out the next growth step.

Endurance Technologies is a two-wheeler and four-wheeler component maker (castings, suspension, braking, transmission). About 76% of its revenue comes from India and 24% from its plants in Italy and Germany, and it benefits directly from the 23-24% growth in Indian 2W and PV volumes. H1 FY27 revenue was ₹9,159 cr, up 31.6% YoY. Our own split, subtracting Q1 (₹4,348 cr, +29.6%) from H1, gives Q2 revenue of about ₹4,811 cr, up roughly 33%. fundamental.thesis: IGL is the main city gas distributor in Delhi NCR, selling CNG to vehicles and piped gas (PNG) to homes and businesses. It is still adding volume: total volumes grew 6.9% YoY to 9.86 MMSCMD in H1 FY27, CNG rose 7.5% and domestic PNG rose 11.5%. Profits, however, have collapsed. H1 FY27 revenue grew 21.4% to ₹10,654 cr, but gas purchase costs jumped 39%, EBITDA margin fell from 12% to 3%, and PAT dropped 71% to ₹211 cr (a 2.0% margin). Q2 alone was much worse: EBITDA was negative ₹31 cr and PAT was about ₹26 cr, down roughly 93% from ₹386 cr a year earlier. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA and P/E, as suits a capital-intensive utility. On those, the stock looks cheap: trailing P/E is 15.4x (inside the 10–18x utilities range), EV/EBITDA is 10.5x and the stock sits around the 12th–15th percentile of the market. But both figures are based on trailing earnings that are falling fast, and analysts have cut current-year EPS estimates by 50–59% in 90 days. So I grade it fair, and the low multiples may be a value trap. The biggest risk is that IGL cannot raise CNG and PNG prices to cover higher gas costs (in a politically sensitive Delhi market, with crude near $91 and rising), so margins stay crushed.

The thesis is undermined by D/E of 37.21×, ₹2,898 cr of goodwill impairments booked in FY26, one subsidiary not on a going-concern basis, 90-day EPS estimate cuts of ~5%, and a RISK_OFF macro regime with Real Estate formally underweighted in sector tilts.

EBITDA fell 5.7% while finance, land and contractor costs all rose. fundamental.thesis: R R Kabel is a mid-sized wires and cables maker with a smaller, loss-making FMEG (fans, lights, appliances) arm. Wires and cables bring in about 91% of H1 revenue (₹5,890 cr, up 54.8%), so the company rides the same power, real-estate and data-centre demand as the bigger cable makers. Growth is strong: H1 FY27 revenue rose 52.8% to ₹6,452 cr and PAT rose 87.2% to ₹386 cr. Taking H1 minus Q1 gives Q2 FY27 revenue of about ₹3,284 cr (+51.8% YoY) and PAT of about ₹181 cr (+56%). That is still faster than the +19.5% of a year ago, but the Q2 PAT margin slipped to about 5.5% from 6.5% in Q1, and EBITDA margin fell from 10.4% to roughly 9.2%. So profitability is rising year on year but has come off its Q1 peak. On EV/EBITDA, the yardstick this sector card calls for, the stock trades at 32.0×, about 37% above the broad-market median (P67). Trailing P/E is 52.7× (P71) against a forward P/E of 34.0×. That multiple sits above the static 28–45× industrials P/E band, but the forward P/E and roughly 21% ROE give a fair, fully priced grade rather than a cheap one, especially with the stock at 94% of its 52-week range. There are no tight cable peers in the comparison set, so the peer rank is only broad-market context. The biggest weakness is cash: H1 operating cash flow was only 0.31× PAT and free cash flow was -₹159 cr. Capex of ₹280 cr in H1 pushed net debt from ₹147 cr to ₹455 cr and finance costs rose 87%. Real leverage is still modest at roughly 0.18× equity; the 13.09 debt/equity figure in the snapshot is most likely a percentage, not a multiple.

Sai Life Sciences is a mid-sized Indian contract research and manufacturing company (CRDMO) serving global pharma. It is moving clients from one-off projects to multi-year relationships covering discovery, development and manufacturing, which should benefit from the China+1 shift. Growth has slowed: H1 FY27 revenue rose 17% YoY to ₹1,213 cr and PAT rose 19% to ₹172 cr, against +29% revenue and +109% PAT in FY26 and +27% revenue in Q3 FY26. Margins have also narrowed, with EBITDA margin falling from 34% in Q3 FY26 to 30% for FY26 and 28% in H1 FY27, and PAT margin falling from 18% to 16% to 14%. Q2 FY27 alone was better at ₹659 cr (+23% YoY), and management expects a stronger second half as new capacity ramps up. Using EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-heavy CDMO, the stock is expensive at 40.6x (P83 vs the broad market). Trailing P/E of 73.5x is well above the 28–40x pharma range, P/B is 10.3x against a 15.1% ROE, and the price sits at 93% of its 52-week range. Analysts raising estimates (+5–6% over 90 days) and a forward P/E of 49x show strong growth is already priced in. The biggest risk is that the ₹621 cr H1 capex and new capacity fill up slower than the lumpy CDMO contract pipeline needs, which would squeeze margins further while the stock trades at a premium.

fundamental.thesis: CIE Automotive India makes forged, cast and machined components for auto OEMs, with about two-thirds of revenue from India and the rest from Europe (it reports on a calendar year, so 9M26 means Jan–Sep 2026). IRCTC is the government-backed monopoly for railway e-ticketing, onboard catering, Rail Neer bottled water and rail tourism, and its ticketing arm has an unusually high 82.4% segment margin. Revenue growth sped up from +3.8% YoY in Q1FY26 and +11.6% in FY26 to +18.1% in Q1FY27 and +17.2% in H1FY27 (₹2,703 cr), led by catering (+30.1%) and tourism (+21.2%). Profit did not keep up: ticketing grew only 0.8%, Rail Neer swung to a ₹95 cr loss, and profit before tax fell 11.3% YoY to ₹798 cr after a ₹116 cr exceptional provision. H1 PAT was not in the extracted data, so the PAT margin is null. Under the sector card's yardstick for a non-platform cash-generating franchise (P/E and EV/EBITDA against peers), the stock is fair: trailing P/E is 30.1x, P41 in the broad market and about 14% below the 35.2x median, while EV/EBITDA of 23.4x sits right at the median (P50). That is well below the sector card's 60–100x norm for consumer discretionary. The stock is at only 10% of its 52-week range, but analysts have cut FY EPS estimates by 8.8% over 90 days, which argues for caution rather than calling it cheap. The main risk is the GSTAT profiteering order: it says ₹5,041 cr plus 18% interest since 2019 (about 12% of market cap and more than the ₹3,709 cr net cash), while only ₹116 cr has been provided. That amount looks large next to Rail Neer's roughly ₹215 cr half-year revenue and may be an extraction error, but until it is checked it is a serious open liability.

ABFRL is a multi-format fashion retailer (Pantaloons value retail, ethnic brands including TCNS, the TMRW digital-brand platform, and luxury retail) with about 1,286 stores. It is no longer the parent of Madura brands like Louis Philippe and Van Heusen, so the remaining portfolio is still loss-making and growing its footprint. The trend is getting worse: Q2 FY27 revenue was ₹2,030 cr, up only 2.4% YoY. Growth has slowed from about +11% in FY26 and Q1 FY27 to +6.4% for H1 and +2.4% for Q2. The Q2 net loss widened 27.5% to ₹376 cr (PAT margin -18.5%, versus -12.3% in Q1). H1 operating margin fell to -7.3% from -2.5% a year ago, and H1 free cash flow was -₹288 cr, so the business is still burning cash. Small bright spots, such as TMRW cutting its EBITDA loss by ₹21 cr in Q1 and luxury growing 30%, do not offset this. P/E means nothing for a loss-maker, so I graded valuation on EV/sales, EV/EBITDA and the direction of unit economics, as the sector card says to do for pre-profit names. Price/sales of 0.92x and P/B of 1.28x (P7 vs the broad market) look cheap on paper. But EV/EBITDA of 18.2x rests on a very thin and shrinking EBITDA base, and ROE is -12.7%, so overall I call it fair, not cheap. The stock is near its 52-week low (19% of range), which may be a value trap rather than a good entry. The biggest risk is that losses keep widening while growth stalls, forcing another round of fundraising or equity dilution.

fundamental.thesis: Amber Enterprises is a contract manufacturer of room-AC parts and complete units, and it is building out an electronics arm (PCBs, defence, railway, mobile phones) through its subsidiary IL JIN, mostly by buying other companies. The latest quarter with usable filing numbers is Q1FY27: revenue of ₹2,663 cr (+7.9% YoY) and PAT of ₹66 cr (-3.4% YoY, 2.5% margin), down from +22% revenue growth in FY26. The pre-computed signals label this 'accelerating', but they read the periods in reverse order, so the real direction is a slowdown. H1FY27 figures did not extract cleanly, and the filing notes point to a consolidated pre-exceptional loss of about ₹10.6 cr, ₹38 cr of damage from the IL JIN factory fire, and ₹9 cr of labour-code costs. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA because this is a capital-heavy manufacturer. At 32.7x EV/EBITDA it sits at P69 vs the market and about 40% above the median, with trailing P/E of 159x (P99) and ROE of only 5.6% against P/B of 6.4x, so the stock is expensive. The forward P/E of 42x assumes a sharp earnings recovery, yet consensus EPS estimates have been cut 8.6% over 90 days while 17 of 23 analysts still rate it a buy, a classic pattern before a stock gets re-rated lower.

fundamental.thesis: Lenskart is India's largest omnichannel eyewear retailer. It designs, makes and sells its own glasses and lenses through company stores and online, and it is growing in the premium consumption segment. Q2 FY27 figures are derived from the official H1 and Q1 filings (H1 revenue ₹5,559 cr minus Q1 ₹2,714 cr, H1 PAT ₹461 cr minus Q1 ₹228 cr). That gives about ₹2,845 cr of revenue, up 32.5% YoY according to the company's press release, and about ₹233 cr of PAT, roughly double last year. Revenue growth slowed from +43.3% in Q1 to +32.5% in Q2, while PAT margin held flat at about 8.2–8.4%, EBITDA margin stayed around 24%, and earnings were well backed by cash (H1 operating cash flow was 1.84x PAT). Valuation is graded on EV/EBITDA and P/E against the sector card's 60–100x premium-consumer band, because no store-level economics (same-store sales growth, store payback) were provided. The stock is expensive: trailing P/E of 181.8x, forward P/E of 95.5x and EV/EBITDA of 90.6x are all at the 97th–99th percentile of the market, and the price sits at 94% of its 52-week range, so even 17% upward revisions to analyst estimates leave consensus targets only about 5% above the current price. The biggest risk is that growth keeps slowing from the 40%s toward the 20%s while the stock is priced for perfection, which could cut the multiple by 25–40%, the typical reset for this sector.

fundamental.thesis: Kalyan Jewellers is one of India's largest listed jewellery retailers, with a national showroom network and a franchise-led expansion model, so it benefits from the premiumisation shift in discretionary spending. H1FY27 revenue was about ₹19,300 cr, up 35.9% YoY, and PAT was ₹716 cr, up 36.4%. But growth is slowing, even though the pre-computed signal says 'accelerating': Q1FY27 grew 45.7%, and the implied Q2 revenue of roughly ₹8,700–9,050 cr (H1 total minus Q1, cross-checked with yfinance) points to only about +11–16% YoY. Q2 PAT of about ₹427 cr also includes a one-off land-sale gain of ₹73 cr, so underlying earnings are weaker than the headline. Using P/E and EV/EBITDA as the yardstick (asset-light retail with stable profits), the stock trades at 29.3x trailing earnings, 20.4x forward and 19.6x EV/EBITDA, all about 12–17% below the broad-market median (around P40) and far below the 60–100x the sector card cites for premium consumer names. With the price at 19% of its 52-week range, cash conversion strong (H1 operating cash flow 1.79x PAT, FCF ₹1,091 cr) and analysts raising estimates (FY EPS +6.7% over 90 days), we grade it fair, leaning cheap. The biggest risk is that the sharp Q2 slowdown reflects gold-price-driven demand weakness rather than a one-quarter blip, while thin margins (PAT 3.7%, EBITDA margin down from 7.9% to 7.4%) and high debt (debt/equity of about 97%, likely including gold metal loans) leave little room for error.

fundamental.thesis: Physicswallah is a fast-growing Indian test-prep and edtech company that sells online courses and runs a growing chain of offline coaching centres. Note that yfinance tags it FMCG, which is wrong; it belongs under Consumer Discretionary. On the latest quarter we could verify from filings (Q1 FY27), revenue was about ₹1,054 cr, up 24.4% YoY. That is slower than the 35.0% growth for full-year FY26, and EBITDA margin fell from 14.1% (FY26) to 4.9% in Q1, while FY26 PAT was a ₹24 cr loss. The Q2 FY27 results were filed on 2026-11-04 but have not been extracted into our trend table. The unverified yfinance Q2 figures (₹738 cr revenue, ₹144 cr PAT) cannot be relied on, and the store-count KPI drop from 353 to 273 looks inconsistent. Because the business is barely profitable, we grade valuation on EV/sales and EV/EBITDA rather than P/E. At 8.4× price/sales and 72× EV/EBITDA (P96 vs the broad market), with a 55.7× forward P/E and ROE of -0.8%, the stock is expensive. The biggest risk is that consensus EPS estimates are being cut (-5.8% in 30 days) while 7 of 10 analysts still rate it a buy, plus integration risk from the new Utkarsh Classes acquisition. Together these set up a classic derating if margins don't recover.

fundamental.thesis: Saregama owns one of India's largest music catalogues and earns from licensing it to streaming, short-video and broadcast platforms, alongside film/video content and live events; it is a mid-cap content franchise that yfinance mislabels as Telecom. The Q2FY27 results announcement (4 Nov 2026) shows revenue from operations of ₹314.3 cr, up 37% YoY, adjusted EBITDA of ₹118 cr (+39%) and PBT of ₹85.8 cr (+43%). That is a sharp rebound from FY26, when revenue fell 15.9% to ₹985 cr, although PAT margin did improve from 18.4% in H1FY26 to 21.0% for full-year FY26. On valuation, using EV/EBITDA and P/E against the broad market because there are no tight listed peers, the stock trades at 25.5x EV/EBITDA (P58) and 43.9x trailing P/E (P64), with a 32.3x forward P/E implying expected earnings growth, so it is fairly valued with modest upside. The biggest risk is cash conversion: CFO/PAT was only 0.48x in FY26 and free cash flow was negative (₹-114 cr) because of heavy spending on acquiring catalogue and content, and the 37% jump is a single quarter off a weak base.

Q2FY27 revenue rose 16.9% YoY to Rs 2,870 cr and PAT rose to Rs 170 cr from about Rs 15 cr, with PAT margin improving from 0.1% in Q3FY26 to 5.8% in Q1FY27 and 5.9% in Q2FY27; however, growth slowed from +23.7% in Q1, the table's 'accelerating' signal mainly reflects a low base, and revenue is only about back to its implied Q2FY25 level. Valuation is fair using EV/EBITDA as the main yardstick: 23.2x is in line with the 23.3x broad-market median (P49), forward P/E of 22.5x is also mid-pack (P48), and the 71.6x trailing P/E (P84) looks inflated by depressed earnings, as the latest quarter annualises to about 29x; trading at 92% of the 52-week range limits upside, while the consensus target data looks unreliable because it does not reconcile with that range. The biggest risk is that the recovery has only two quarters of evidence, and this analysis had no usable management guidance or Q2 EBITDA margin to test its durability.

fundamental.thesis: Whirlpool of India is a leading single-segment home appliances manufacturer (refrigerators, washing machines, ACs) with a well-established urban franchise, though it faces intensifying competition from Haier, LG, and listed peers. Revenue inflected positively in Q1FY27 to ₹2,727 cr (+12.1% YoY consolidated, PDF-sourced), reversing prior weakness (-3.8% in Q2FY26, -1.0% in 9MFY26) — a genuine top-line recovery — but PAT collapsed -29.6% YoY to ₹103 cr with EBITDA margin compressing sharply to 7.62% from 9.77%, meaning the company is growing revenues while simultaneously destroying earnings quality. At 34.84× trailing P/E (P49 vs broad-market peers, median), EV/EBITDA of 19.1× (P39, below median), and P/B of 2.5× against a meagre 7.24% ROE (FY26), the stock is fairly valued on headline multiples but expensive on a quality-adjusted basis — a company with sub-8% ROE and accelerating downward EPS revisions (-25.2% over 90 days) does not merit a median consumer-discretionary multiple. The biggest risk is that margins continue to deteriorate under rising crude-driven input cost pressure while aggressive sell-side estimate cuts (-25.2% in 90 days) signal further earnings-led de-rating from an already distressed 7.1% of 52-week range.

fundamental.thesis: Zee Entertainment is India's second-largest broadcast media group (~50 TV channels plus the ZEE5 OTT platform), structurally pressured by the secular migration to streaming and left exposed after the Jiostar/Sony merger collapsed; it now carries substantial governance and legal overhangs that suppress any re-rating. FY26 annual revenue declined 1.9% YoY to ₹7,567 Cr while PAT collapsed 82.8% to ₹120 Cr, compressing PAT margin to 1.6% and EBITDA margin to a catastrophic 2.6% (from 13.4% in FY25) — the multi-quarter trajectory shows revenue decelerating and margins contracting across every available period with no stabilisation evident in filings. Forward P/E of 13.42× (P19 vs broad-market peers, -42% below median) and P/B of 0.9× (P2 vs peers, -80% below median) both screen as unambiguously cheap; EV/EBITDA of 23× looks deceptively at median but is computed on severely depressed EBITDA — on normalised 12-13% margins the implied EV/EBITDA would be sub-5×, confirming franchise-level cheapness if operational recovery is achievable. The single largest risk to the recovery thesis is the IDBI Bank insolvency petition (filed September 2025) seeking NCLT-admitted CIRP initiation, which if granted would be existential for the business regardless of underlying brand and content-IP value.

fundamental.thesis: Patanjali Foods is India's largest edible oils company (formerly Ruchi Soya), with a fast-growing FMCG overlay spanning biscuits, nutrition, and home/personal care under the Patanjali brand — but edible oils still account for roughly 70%+ of revenues, making this a commodity-FMCG hybrid rather than a pure compounder, and that matters critically for how to frame the valuation. Q1FY27 delivered record revenue of ₹11,337 cr (+29.3% YoY, accelerating from +20.9% in Q2FY26) and PAT of ₹336 cr (+86.1% YoY), but underlying quality is deteriorating: gross margin compressed from 15.26% (Q2FY26) to 13.42% (Q1FY27), EBITDA margin fell from 6.2% to 4.8%, and PAT margin contracted to 3.0% — a persistent multi-quarter contraction signal that runs counter to the top-line acceleration. At trailing P/E 25.43×, the stock screens cheap versus the FMCG sector benchmark of 40–60×, but the discount is structurally warranted by the commodity-heavy business mix; EV/EBITDA of 25× (P55 vs broad-market peers) and P/E peer rank of P32 both point to fair value rather than genuine mispricing, and the sector card's own caution — 'cheap FMCG usually means a structural problem' — applies directly here. The overriding risk is extreme balance sheet leverage (D/E 21.3×) combined with negative FCF (CFO/PAT −1.13× in Q2FY26) — at a 5.29% US 10Y yield and with PAT margins at 3%, any commodity cost spike or interest burden increase could rapidly destroy earnings entirely.

In Q2FY27, total income rose 14.8% YoY to ₹45,674 cr and PAT rose 39.4% to ₹7,705 cr. Revenue growth has picked up from about +4% (H1FY26) to +7% (Q1FY27) to +15%, and loan growth has risen from 11.9% to 19.3%, but the PAT jump is flattered by a weak Q2FY26 base (₹5,528 cr), and the PAT margin slipped from 17.7% in Q1 to 16.9%. On the lender yardstick from the sector card (P/B against sustainable ROE), a P/B of 1.83x for a TTM ROE of 13.2% is fair: it is above the peer median of 1.5x (P64), while trailing P/E of 15.0x is about 11% below peers (P43). That fits a bank whose asset quality has improved (GNPA down from 1.46% to 1.23%) but whose returns are only moderate. The biggest risk is that loans are now growing faster than deposits: the loan-to-deposit ratio is a stretched 98.7%, credit cost has risen from 0.20% to 0.72%, and provision coverage is slipping (70.5% to 70.0%). Together these point to future funding-cost and NIM pressure, and the extracted NIM readings (3.42% in Q1 vs 2.32% in Q2) conflict too much to confirm the NIM recovery the sector card expects.

fundamental.thesis: POWERGRID is India's dominant inter-state power transmission company, earning a regulated return on equity (about 15.5%) on assets it puts into service, so earnings depend on how fast new lines are commissioned rather than on power prices. Growth has been flat: H1 FY27 revenue rose 2.8% YoY to ₹23,313 cr and PAT rose 3.7% to ₹7,465 cr. The implied Q2 FY27 is revenue of ₹11,816 cr (about +2.9% YoY) and PAT of about ₹3,867 cr, a 32.7% margin, after Q1 grew revenue 2.7% with PAT down 0.9%. ₹18,913 cr of H1 capex should be commissioned over time and lift the asset base, but that has not shown up in reported growth yet. For a regulated utility I value it on P/B against ROE, with EV/EBITDA as a cross-check. P/B of 2.64x for 16.5% TTM ROE (13.98% annualised H1) is fair, and both trailing P/E (14.2x, inside the 10–18x utilities range) and EV/EBITDA (10.7x) sit at the 25th percentile of peers (P25), only 3–7% below the sector median, so overall it is fair, not clearly cheap. A forward P/E slightly above trailing and 90-day EPS estimate cuts (-2.2% for this year, -3.3% for next) point to flat earnings, with the roughly 3–5% dividend yield as the main return floor. The biggest risk is that growth stays near 3% if new lines are commissioned slowly, while leverage stays high (debt/equity 1.42, ₹1.51L cr of borrowings) and free cash flow is slightly negative because of capex.

fundamental.thesis: Sundaram Finance is a conservatively run, mid-sized Chennai NBFC focused mainly on vehicle finance, with housing finance, asset management and a general-insurance JV (Royal Sundaram) under the group; it is known for steady growth and clean asset quality. H1FY27 consolidated PAT rose 20% to Rs 1,153 cr, and standalone Q2 PAT grew 21% to Rs 475 cr on 28% disbursement growth and 19% core AUM growth, with Gross Stage 3 improving to 1.84% from 2.03% and provision cover rising to 51% from 45%. However, momentum slowed within the half: consolidated PAT growth fell from +33.9% in Q1 to roughly +9% implied for Q2 (Rs 517 cr vs Rs 474 cr), and Q2 standalone profits from operations grew only 11%, partly because of a Rs 66 cr Supreme Court-driven motor third-party provision at Royal Sundaram. Using the lender yardstick of price-to-book against ROE, valuation looks fair to full: 3.5x book for a 16.75% ROE sits at P67 of peers on P/B and at P100 on forward P/E (21.2x vs a 14.6x median), so the quality premium is already priced in, and sell-side EPS estimates have been cut 1.4-1.8% over 90 days. The main risks are that this premium unwinds if the slower Q2 profit growth persists, and leadership transition after the chairman's resignation on 2026-11-05.

fundamental.thesis: Fortis Healthcare runs a large hospital network of about 6,300 operational beds plus a diagnostics arm of about 400 labs, and it grows through occupancy, revenue per patient and adding beds. In Q2 FY27, revenue rose 17.3% YoY to Rs 2,735 cr, with growth essentially flat over five periods (17.3% to 17.8%, with only a slight recent easing), helped by 72% hospital occupancy and about 7% growth in revenue per patient, but PAT fell 2.5% to Rs 320 cr and PAT margin dropped from 14.1% to 11.7%; lower exceptional gains (Rs 3 cr vs Rs 24 cr) explain only about 1 point of that drop, and even excluding them PAT grew only about 4% by my pre-tax-unadjusted estimate. Using EV/EBITDA as the yardstick for this capital-intensive business, the stock is expensive at 35.6x vs a sector median of 23.3x (P81), and a trailing P/E of 69.3x vs a forward P/E of 40.9x implies about 69% EPS growth, although the mostly pharma peer set makes the comparison imperfect and the 34% consensus upside looks overstated because the 52-week position implies a price near Rs 957, or about 15% upside to the Rs 1,098 mean target. The biggest risk is that revenue growth keeps failing to reach profit while FY EPS estimates, already cut 5.8% over 90 days, fall further against a valuation that needs a sharp earnings rebound.

The Q2FY27 results filed on 4 Nov have not been extracted, and the unverified yfinance rows do not hang together (Q2FY27 revenue ₹1,957 cr against a FY26 run-rate near ₹2,700 cr a quarter, and an outlier Q1FY27 PAT of ₹451 cr), so the current trajectory cannot be confirmed. fundamental.thesis: Tube Investments of India is a high-ROIC diversified engineering conglomerate (core segment ROCE 44–49%) spanning precision tubes, metal-formed products, industrial chains, a 56.3% stake in CG Power (power equipment), and a nascent EV mobility business — positioning it across India's capital-goods and energy-transition cycles. Q1FY27 consolidated revenue grew +17.1% YoY to ₹6,215 cr (consistent with FY26's +17.5%), but PAT declined -3.0% YoY to ₹294 cr as PAT margin compressed to 4.73% from 5.71% YoY — EBITDA margin has contracted sequentially from 12.6% (9M FY26) to 11.6% (FY26) to 10.6% (Q1FY27), driven primarily by the EV segment's ₹147 cr PBT loss in the quarter. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive conglomerate (27.4× vs sector peer median 34.0×, P29 percentile), the stock grades fair; trailing P/E of 84.75× sits at P88 vs peers and well above the Industrials ceiling of 45×, but this is inflated by EV-loss-suppressed current earnings, and forward P/E of 35.05× (near sector median) implies the market is already pricing in meaningful earnings recovery — leaving limited valuation buffer if that recovery is delayed. The biggest near-term risk is the EV segment burning roughly ₹147 cr in PBT per quarter with no stated path to breakeven, while sell-side EPS estimates have been cut -12% over both 30 and 90 days — a warning that consensus may need further downward adjustment before a re-rating.

fundamental.thesis: Dixon Technologies is India's largest contract electronics maker (EMS). It assembles smartphones, TVs, lighting, IT hardware and telecom gear, and is building camera-module and display capacity under the PLI scheme and the China+1 shift. The filed H1 FY27 figures show revenue of ₹37,938 cr and PAT of ₹1,129 cr, with PAT up 51% YoY. That leaves an implied Q2 of about ₹21,900–22,400 cr revenue and ₹411–466 cr PAT, which is only about a 2% PAT margin against 4.3–4.5% in Q1 FY27. Q1 revenue grew +21% to +25% (the two extracted Q1 rows disagree). The reported +147% H1 revenue growth and the ₹4,959 cr FY26 row do not reconcile with the quarterly figures, so the growth rate cannot be trusted. Margins are being diluted as volume grows faster than profit. Because this is an assembly-heavy, low-margin business, I graded on EV/EBITDA plus trailing P/E. EV/EBITDA is 32.3x, and trailing P/E of 42.9x sits at the top of the 28–45x Industrials range, so I grade it fair-to-full rather than cheap even though the stock is only 22% up its 52-week range. The peer-rank block compares Dixon with IT-services companies (WIPRO, INFY, PERSISTENT), which are not real peers, so I gave its 'P100 expensive' verdict little weight. The forward P/E is above the trailing P/E, and analysts have cut FY EPS estimates by 7% over 30 days and 10% over 90 days while ratings stay 22 buy. That pattern often comes before a de-rating. FY26 cash conversion was also weak: cash from operations was only 0.22x PAT and free cash flow was -₹271 cr.

Tata Chemicals sells soda ash, which makes it a global price taker, with plants in India, the US, the UK and Kenya; it also has a smaller consumer and specialty arm (Living Essentials, Rallis). Sales are recovering, with growth of +13.9% in Q1FY27 and +11.0% for H1FY27 (₹8,432 cr), after -1% to -2% across Q3FY26 to Q4FY26. Profit has not followed: H1 PAT fell 98% to ₹10 cr (₹535 cr a year ago), and Q2FY27 alone was an estimated loss of about ₹50 cr on about ₹4,177 cr of sales, against a ₹219 cr profit in Q2FY26. EBITDA margin also slipped from 13.0% in Q1 to an implied ~9.2% in Q2, hurt by UK gas costs, the Kenya suspension and weak soda ash prices. There is no trailing P/E because profits are negative, so I graded on the sector card's yardstick for commodity chemicals (EV/EBITDA plus balance sheet). At 14.5x EV/EBITDA the stock costs roughly double the 5–8x mid-cycle norm, though that is partly because EBITDA is at a cyclical low. P/B of 0.82x is the cheapest in the sector (P0), so overall I call it fair, not a clear bargain. The main reason for caution is that analysts have cut this year's EPS forecasts by 55% in 90 days and their ratings lean sell (4 sell vs 2 buy).

fundamental.thesis: Angel One is one of India's largest retail stockbrokers by active clients, so it earns mainly from broking fees (heavily F&O-linked), interest on client margin funding and distribution. That makes it a high-beta bet on market activity, not a lender. The latest extracted quarter is Q1FY27, where revenue rose +25.4% YoY to ₹1,430 cr and PAT doubled (+102%) to ₹231 cr, with PAT margin up from 10.0% to 16.2%. But this follows a weak FY26 (revenue -1.9%, PAT -21.9%), so much of the rebound is a recovery from a low base rather than proven new growth. The Q2FY27 results filed on 2026-10-15 are not yet in the extracted data. For a fee-based broker I graded on P/E cross-checked with P/B against ROE: trailing P/E of 35.8x is above the 18–28x NBFC/capital-markets band and in line with the broad market (P52), while forward P/E of 20.3x prices in a further earnings recovery. P/B of 5.25x against only 15.5% ROE is rich, so overall this is fair at best, with the stock at 97% of its 52-week range and FY EPS estimates cut 3.5% in 30 days and 4.8% in 90 days. The biggest risk is regulatory: further SEBI tightening of retail F&O, or a drop in market activity in this risk-off tape, would hit volumes directly. Cash flow from operations was also deeply negative in FY26 (-4.5x PAT) because the borrowed-money margin-funding book grew about 39%, which adds leverage (debt/equity about 1.0–1.3x).

Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive model per the sector card, 45.51× sits at the upper bound of the 28–45× Industrials range and at P86 in the broad market (95% premium to median), grading expensive; the forward P/E discount (33.25× vs 54× trailing) signals the street is pricing in a sharp earnings recovery — but that recovery has not yet appeared in filed numbers and Q1 FY27 extraction is blank despite the August 2026 filing date. The single biggest risk is that margin compression deepens further on the ISRF ramp and rising crude-linked operating costs, in a RISK_OFF macro with D/E at 28.47 — any slippage in earnings recovery would unwind the current rich valuation quickly.

fundamental.thesis: GMR Airports is India's largest private airport operator, running Delhi, Hyderabad, Goa (Mopa), Medan, and newly Nagpur and Vizag. Its earnings depend on regulated aero tariffs plus a fast-growing non-aero business (retail, F&B, real estate, hotels). Revenue growth has slowed sharply: from +48.6% YoY in Q3FY26 to +23.0% in Q1FY27, and to about +11.6% in Q2FY27 (implied ₹4,188 cr, from H1 ₹8,273 cr minus Q1 ₹4,085 cr). EBITDA margin has slipped from 43.8% to 37.9% and passenger traffic grew only about 1%, so growth now rests on tariffs and non-aero income. Implied Q2 PAT is only about ₹65 cr (1.6% margin) after ₹1,931 cr of H1 interest, and yfinance shows a ₹15 cr loss, so profit quality is thin. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA because this is a capital-intensive, regulated-asset business and P/E is not meaningful: at 25.1x EV/EBITDA, 82.6x forward P/E (P98 among peers), negative book value and 98% of the 52-week range, it is expensive. Sell-side EPS estimates have also been cut 37–42% over 90 days while 7 of 8 ratings stay Buy, a classic sign of a possible de-rating. The biggest risk is that weak traffic (Hyderabad -11.7%, Mopa -14.4%) plus a heavy debt load leaves the stock leaning on the Delhi CP-4 tariff being implemented on time.

fundamental.thesis: Graphite India makes graphite electrodes for electric-arc-furnace (EAF) steelmakers. It runs 80,000 tpa of capacity at 97% utilisation, and that demand depends on the steel cycle and on EAF adoption, not on an order book, so the Industrials order-book framework fits poorly. H1 FY27 consolidated revenue rose 34% YoY to Rs 1,871 cr and PAT rose 26% to Rs 265 cr; subtracting Q1 (Rs 842 cr / Rs 171 cr) implies Q2 FY27 revenue of about Rs 1,029 cr (+41% YoY vs Rs 729 cr) and PAT of about Rs 94 cr (+24% vs Rs 76 cr). However, the implied Q2 PAT margin fell sharply to about 9.1% from 20.3% in Q1, so revenue is accelerating while profitability per rupee is slipping. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the yardstick for this capital-intensive business, and the signals conflict, so the grade is fair: EV/EBITDA of 51x (P89, +119% vs median) and a trailing P/E of 72x look expensive because trailing earnings come from the FY26 trough (PAT -62%), while a forward P/E of 12.5x (P16), P/B of 2.2x, and a mid-range 52-week position price in a sharp earnings recovery that the 30-day sell-side EPS upgrade (+8.3%) supports. The main risk is that the recovery stalls as margins compress, global steel output stays flat (-0.2% YoY, China -1.6%), and Chinese electrode pricing pressure persists; the reported debt/equity of 6.27 also conflicts with the company's historically low leverage and is probably a units error, but it should be verified.

fundamental.thesis: Jindal Stainless (JSL) is India's #1 stainless steel producer and #5 globally ex-China, operating 4.2 MTPA capacity across 120+ product grades on a ~₹44,000 cr TTM revenue base, with strong structural demand from government infrastructure programmes (railways, highways, airports). Q1FY27 revenue grew +10.5% YoY to ₹11,279 cr (stable, not accelerating from FY26's +9.3%), but PAT margin has contracted from 7.4% in FY26 to 6.8% in Q1FY27 as raw material costs at ~70% of revenue compress the spread; PAT growth has decelerated sharply from +27.4% in FY26 to +7.7% YoY in Q1FY27. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick (the correct metric for capital-intensive steel, per sector card), JSL trades at 6.59× — inside the 5–8× mid-cycle cyclical range and at the 4th percentile vs 473 broad-market peers — grading CHEAP, corroborated by forward P/E (13.68×) sitting at a discount to trailing P/E (18.27×), pricing in continued earnings growth. The biggest risk to this thesis is raw material cost volatility (nickel, ferro-alloys at ~70% of revenue) combined with structural Chinese overcapacity, which could further erode the already-contracting EBITDA margin (13.1% Q1FY27 vs 13.7% peak in FY26).

fundamental.thesis: Paradeep Phosphates is a mid-sized Indian phosphatic and complex fertiliser maker (about 3.7 MT capacity running near full utilisation, 18 states, around 12 mn farmers). It is a commodity-spread business exposed to sulphur, ammonia and phosphoric-acid costs and to government subsidy timing, so it should be judged on EBITDA per tonne rather than on volume. Q2FY27 revenue grew only +7% YoY to ₹7,364 cr, slowing sharply from +49% in Q2FY26 and +36% in Q1FY27, while PAT fell 64% YoY to ₹122 cr and PAT margin compressed from 5.0% to 1.7%; EBITDA margin halved from 10.2% to 5.8% on sulphur cost and availability pressure. On the capital-intensive yardstick, EV/EBITDA of 9.9x is above the card's 5–8x mid-cycle range for chemical cyclicals, while trailing P/E of 15.3x sits inside the 12–22x Materials band; I grade it fair, not cheap. The 'cheap vs peers' signal comes from a broad-market comparison with no fertiliser peers, and the trailing multiple is flattered by earlier high-margin quarters while FY EPS estimates were cut about 28% in 30 days. The biggest risk is that the margin squeeze persists while working capital balloons: H1FY27 free cash flow was -₹2,625 cr with CFO/PAT of -4.5x, likely from subsidy receivables and inventory build, on a balance sheet with roughly 1x debt/equity.

fundamental.thesis: Cohance Lifesciences is an Indian CDMO/API platform (formerly Suven Pharmaceuticals) serving global pharma innovators across Pharma CDMO, API+, Sapala nucleic-acid specialty chemicals, and Formulations — a niche franchise currently navigating a sharp operational trough driven by post-merger NJ Bio consolidation, Pharma CDMO order phasing, and Specialty Chemicals destocking. Q1FY27 consolidated revenue declined 23.1% YoY to ₹422 cr (decelerating sharply from +12.5% in Q1FY26 and extending the -13.1% full-year FY26 decline), with Pharma CDMO down 38.7% YoY, NJ Bio contributing an EBITDA loss of ₹328 mn, and PAT swinging to ₹-45 cr (-176% YoY); EBITDA margins imploded 2,220bps to 2.2%, though gross margins held at 71.5% and FCF remained a healthy ₹106 cr — indicating the trough is volume/timing-driven rather than structural margin destruction, and management has guided Q1FY27 as the floor with H2FY27 YoY recovery. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick per sector card guidance for a capital-intensive CDMO, the stock trades at 39.3× (P81 vs broad-market peers, 68% premium to median 23.3×), expensive on any normalised basis; trailing P/E of 88.6× (P91, distorted by the trough PAT) and forward P/E of 38.9× still sit well above sector Pharma medians of 28–40×, while sell-side FY EPS estimates have been cut 25.5% in the last 30 days — suggesting the recovery the market is paying for is actively being revised downward. The biggest risk is binary: an active FDA Warning Letter at the Nacharam FDF facility, if not resolved swiftly, could trigger customer qualification audits across the CDMO business precisely when the recovery pipeline depends on securing and delivering new orders against a backdrop of dangerously high Debt/Equity of 9.93.
